title: An Astute SNL Sketch About Who Deals With Aging Parents
excerpt: Like a lot of Millennials coming to terms with the inevitability of elder care, John Mulaney is thinking about Baby Boomers
body: Like a lot of Millennials coming to terms with the inevitability of elder care, John Mulaney is thinking about Baby Boomers
The aging generation came up throughout last night’s episode of Saturday Night Live , the 44-year-old Mulaney’s seventh as host

He teased Boomers in his monologue, claiming that all of the complaints they have about Gen Z are actually true of Boomers: They, too, are addicted to technology, behave toxically online, and melt down when they feel ignored

Continuing the ribbing, one sketch portrayed a group of younger Boomers at Woodstock; Mulaney’s character, bedecked in a frizzy wig and a brown fringe jacket, imagined the houses and money they could amass in the future. “I feel like we should get as much of it as we can and then just, like, have it,” he said, to the confusion of his weed-smoking hippie friends. (Yes, it was a very on-the-nose bit about how Boomers left their flower-power ideals in the 1960s.) But Mulaney’s motif played out most effectively in the pretaped sketch “Sister.” This spoof on a pharmaceutical ad proposes a solution to the problem of finding high-quality care for elderly parents : “I didn’t know where to turn,” a smug Mulaney says of his trouble helping his father. “That’s when I heard about Sister”—Mulaney’s character’s actual sister, that is

After “years of internalized sexism” warping her brain, the ad notes, a simple text message will compel Sister to leave her life behind for the responsibility of live-in, unpaid, around-the-clock care
The tendency of older female siblings to take on practical and emotional labor in their family unit has become an observable phenomenon in social-science research, and something of a meme too
In the sketch, as in life, they need not even be the eldest—societal pressures on women can work on daughters generally

The sketch was pointed about the fact that children can love their ailing parents without loving the extra work of elder care—especially when it means navigating complex systems such as health care. “Speak to human
Speak to human ,” a Sister, portrayed by Jane Wickline, says forcefully into a phone

Those tasks can be difficult for anyone—but some people pawn them off on siblings. “I used to get overwhelmed by my dad’s medications,” says Kenan Thompson’s character, but it’s not a problem for Sister—or, if it is, she hasn’t brought it up
The sketch highlights not just the central unfairness of women taking on this kind of care work but the hurtful resentments that build over time in these situations
The father in the ad comments on his daughter’s weight out of the blue and complains about her control of his salt intake

Sister’s husband can also be looped into the work, but when he asks about why they had to upend their lives, Sister’s reply is forceful: “Because he’s my dad, that’s why!” [ Read: The parenting prophecy ] Judging from the attention the sketch is getting this morning, its portrayal of a growing elderly population’s strain on many families resonated with viewers

If you listen closely, the sketch offers a solution of sorts: A disclaimer at the end of the ad says that the offer on Sister is void if she “has a good therapist.” Mulaney got more specific about a Boomer in his own life during his monologue

He discussed how deciding his father is autistic has “cleared up everything about our childhoods”—even explaining behaviors such as shaking hands with a baby or trying to make small talk about the fullness of a trash can (with a 4-year-old)
One notable Baby Boomer with a penchant for rambling tangents was absent from this week’s SNL : Donald Trump
The cold open instead riffed on Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy

Mulaney’s CIA officer tried to warn tech billionaires such as Mark Zuckerberg (Andrew Dismukes) and Elon Musk (Jeremy Culhane) about the dangers of honey traps, insisting that there was no overlap between their interests and those of beautiful women
Those guys are not Boomers—the youngest, Sam Altman (played here by Ben Marshall), is 41—but in the sketch, they didn’t seem to be able to understand the lesson

title: The Pentagon Ignored a Warning About the Danger of Iran’s Drones
excerpt: F rom a distance , the Iranian drone resembled an arrowhead, pointing downward as it dove out of the sky
body: F rom a distance , the Iranian drone resembled an arrowhead, pointing downward as it dove out of the sky
Its propeller, powered by the kind of motor typically used in dirt bikes and lawnmowers, produced a high-pitched wail
It struck midmorning on March 1, the second day of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran, hitting a logistics center in Kuwait used by the American military
Dozens of personnel from the Army Reserve were working at an office building there
The incoming drone, a variant of the Shahed, slammed through the roof of the building and detonated its payload
Six American service members were killed and more than two dozen wounded, several of them critically—the deadliest attack on U.S. troops in the war
It will be hard for the survivors to forget the drone’s distinctive noise
In Ukraine, which has faced years of attacks from this type of drone, people often compare its sound as it falls out of the sky to a Vespa revving its engine
But the noise no longer terrifies Ukrainians the way it once did
Last year, Ukraine’s arms industry developed a cheap and effective way to shoot down Shaheds
The U.S. military knew about this technology months before the war in Iran began

A group of senior American officers, worried about exactly the type of attack that killed those six soldiers in Kuwait, told me they repeatedly urged commanders in the Middle East to deploy the new Ukrainian technology
The Pentagon ignored their warnings, which included detailed reports sent up the chain of command
Several of the officers who tried to raise the alarm about Iranian Shaheds have since been fired or forced into early retirement

In a statement, the Pentagon disputed the officers’ account and said it was “disgusting” for the Atlantic to suggest that the U.S. military was “somehow unprepared” for the start of the war in Iran. “Central Command established the most extensive air defense umbrella in the world over the Middle East,” Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell wrote in the statement. “Make no mistake: The U.S. military has the best offensive and defensive capabilities of any nation on Earth, and we always protect our bases and our people.” The warnings were based on Ukraine’s experience with Russia, which acquired Shahed drones from Iran in 2022
Waves of them have pounded Ukrainian cities ever since, often in swarms of a few hundred per night
Last summer, the armed forces of Ukraine deployed a new type of interceptor to destroy Shaheds in midair
Army officers stationed in Germany began training on these interceptors that fall, and they asked their Ukrainian allies to produce a report about their new invention

The document, dated December 2025, was titled in the military’s turgid style: “Operational Experience in the Employment of UAV Interceptors in Countering Shahed-Type Aerial Threats.” It described in detail how Ukraine had developed these defensive weapons
A drawing of an interceptor appeared on the cover of the report, alongside a Shahed with a bull’s-eye on its belly
It was shared inside the military and with some U.S. allies in December, roughly two months before the war in Iran started
The Army’s European Command, led at the time by General Chris “C.D.” Donahue, had by then deployed the new interceptors at bases in Europe, including in Romania and Poland

Donahue and his team in Wiesbaden, Germany, urged their fellow officers to do the same at bases in other regions, especially in the Middle East, where the threat from Iranian drones seemed most obvious to them
The officers in Wiesbaden sent the document up to their commanders, and they pressed the leadership in Washington to act on it
Had their warnings been heeded, they believe the lives of U.S. soldiers could have been saved

Looking back, some of the officers still wonder whether they could have done more to protect those six Americans in Kuwait. “This should all have been figured out beforehand,” one of them told me. “How are we going to defend against Shaheds?” At the start of this year, the team of officers in Wiesbaden compiled a second report about the Ukrainian interceptors
To ensure the widest possible distribution, the military cleared it for public release in February
The document, roughly 12 pages long, described how European Command had fielded the Ukrainian interceptors at some of its bases
It offered detailed guidance for commanders in other regions to do the same
No one involved in preparing the two reports knew the timing of the U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran, which was then widely reported to be in the works
But they understood that any Iranian response would almost certainly involve Shahed drones, which the regime had invented, mass produced, and stockpiled
The second report was published on February 23, too late, as it turned out, for its warnings to make much difference

The war in Iran would start only five days later. [ Read: The glaring oversight in the U.S. war plan ] This account of the Pentagon’s failure to defend against these weapons is based on interviews with more than a dozen current and former military officers from the U.S. and Ukraine, who were involved in the effort to warn about the danger of Iranian drones and arm U.S. forces with the most effective countermeasures
Most of them spoke on condition of anonymity, because they fear reprisals from their commanders and officials at the Pentagon
Since taking office last year, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has overseen the widespread use of polygraph tests to find and punish military officers who speak with journalists without permission
He has also ordered the military to cut 20 percent of the positions reserved for generals and admirals across the armed forces
Donahue fell victim to that purge this summer

In the final months of his Army career, he worked with the team in Wiesbaden to send hundreds of Ukrainian interceptors to the Middle East, hoping they could defend against another deadly strike on U.S. forces
Hegseth did not support these efforts, the officers involved told me. “The technology is so effective

But the top officials in Washington did not want to accept it: “Because of arrogance, they said, Why do we need it? ” B y now , nearly five years after Russia invaded, most U.S. military officers would agree that Ukraine offers important lessons on the future of warfare

title: What Are the Masculine Virtues?
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube One of the things that President Trump seems to admire most about his embattled defense secretary is Pete Heg
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube One of the things that President Trump seems to admire most about his embattled defense secretary is Pete Hegseth’s vision of warrior masculinity, a vision Hegseth has attempted to impose on the military, through the firing of qualified high-ranking female officers, the denigration of long-established rules of engagement, and even the proposed screening of service members’ testosterone levels

These efforts are taking place at a time when many young American men are facing a very real crisis, but they don’t seem to have landed among their target audience: Male voters younger than 30 swung 40 percent toward Democrats in the midterms, one of the election’s largest such demographic shifts

In this episode of The Permanent Questions , David Brooks talks with Phil Klay, a Marine Corps veteran, National Book Award–winning novelist and story writer, and close observer of the effects that our 21st-century wars have had on American soldiers
Klay explains why Hegseth’s version of manhood is bad for men (and the military), why warfare can never be stripped of its moral meaning, and why love is the greatest masculine virtue
The following is a transcript of the episode: David Brooks: There are at least three important things going on in America right now
Lots of young men are out of the labor force entirely
Suicide rates for young men are vastly higher than suicide rates for women
Second, we’re living with the consequences of probably three failed wars in the 21st century
There was the war in Iraq, the war in Afghanistan, and currently the war in Iran
That means there are a lot of young men—and women—who’ve been through those wars, who fought in those wars, who are trying to live with the consequences
This is a culture that is hurting in a lot of different ways
Sometimes I think the Trump administration is a big advertisement for a certain sort of masculinity

It purports to be a solution to our cultural problems—that we’re gonna have a bunch of manly men and womanly women and we’ll return to a kind of gender relations that, according to some people, were healthier
Personally, I’m not particularly thrilled with what Pete Hegseth and Donald Trump are selling
I’d like a different social ideal, especially for guys
I’d like a different masculine ideal than the ones being offered today
To figure out how we could get to a healthier masculinity, I’m gonna hash it out with Phil Klay
He served as a public affairs officer in the Anbar Province between 2007 and 2008 during the surge
When he returned home, he became a writer
His collection of short stories called Redeployment won the National Book Award in 2014
His most recent book of nonfiction essays is Uncertain Ground: Citizenship in an Age of Endless, Invisible War
He was recently selected to become the president of PEN America
It’s a real pleasure to welcome Phil Klay to this table

What should men be like? What should people be like? How do you be honorable? It seems to me there have been a series of social ideals that young men in particular were supposed to follow and this was held up as their social ideal
If you want to be a young man, be like this guy
You go back to ancient Greece, you got Achilles
Then you got Pericles, who’s a magnanimous man
Magnanimous man is kind of aloof and standoffish
You get a very different masculine ideal, which is about compassion and peace
Jewish prophets and sages, which is like an intellectual ideal
You go to the Renaissance, you’ve got the courtier
There was this book—I’ve always wanted to write a book like this—Castiglione
It’s quite something, Brooks: How to be a courtier, how to be elegant and graceful
Klay: Sprezzatura—you do everything effortlessly
Chivalric knights like Lancelot, and that’s an ideal
Then you get the 18th-century Enlightenment
You got a Ben Franklin kinda guy who studies everything on the Earth
Then you get my hero, the gentleman in Trollope, and Trollope novels always revolve around a gentleman who is not highborn necessarily, but who has a virtuous life
And then in one of those interesting cases in American history, it’s the end of the 19th century
America seems to go through a moral panic every time a war generation starts dying

title: ChatGPT Analyzed 32,245 of My Text Messages
excerpt: A few weeks ago, a chatbot read a tranche of my text messages spanning more than a dozen years and declared that I’d been a bad friend
body: A few weeks ago, a chatbot read a tranche of my text messages spanning more than a dozen years and declared that I’d been a bad friend

First, some context: I’m writing a memoir about my love life, or lack thereof, so I’ve been going through old correspondence and quizzing friends about their memories of the years when I was single (2012–22) and not so single (2022–now)

One of those friends is Michael—who, like me, is unmarried; who, like me, has an extensive history of encounters facilitated by dating apps; and who, like me, was long looking for love but often found himself disappointed
My text history with Michael goes back to 2014, when we first met
At other times, we go weeks, months, even a year without communicating (for reasons that have never been entirely clear to us)
Six years ago, I moved from New York, where Michael lives, to Los Angeles, so since then, our friendship has been conducted largely via phone

This means that an already rich history of friendship has become richer, not just because of the accumulation of our shared experiences, but also because of the way our communications have been automatically documented and archived

A text thread, when you think about it, is an incredible repository of primary source material—in effect, a data set—containing clues to how people conduct countless aspects of their lives, whether mundane or profound

For a memoirist, such material can be a gold mine. (I suspect that future historians will agree.) More freewheeling than, say, letters or emails, texts capture the immediacy of a writer’s feelings and observations and, because of that, can seem particularly “authentic.” [ Read: Archivists aren’t ready for the ‘very online’ era ] My initial quest for love-life insights within my archive with Michael yielded somewhat frustrating results
When I searched for words such as guy and date and sex , I quickly became overwhelmed and called him to complain: “There’s too much material for me to handle.” A few minutes later, my phone dinged
Michael had sent me an Excel spreadsheet containing our entire text history and suggested that I upload it into ChatGPT
I’d been playing with chatbots for about a year and a half
For my memoir, I’d used them to pull out important strands from the transcripts of audio and Zoom interviews
I confess that I also once used a chatbot to give me an astrological analysis of a potential romantic relationship
So, with little hesitation, I took Michael’s advice, fed ChatGPT our data, and awaited the results

They weren’t all that surprising, at least when it came to the bot’s analysis of my romantic life. (Among other things, it told me that I had bad taste in men.) But I noticed that it shared some wholly unexpected stuff about my friendship with Michael (for instance: “Neither has to construct a respectable version of the self for the other”)
ChatGPT had expanded its feedback beyond an analysis of my love life to an analysis of the relationship framing the discussions of my love life
I wondered: If I asked it to go deeper on Michael and me, what more might it say? N ever before have we had the means to synthesize, so quickly, words poured unadulterated into a single device

A few years ago, one technologist imported into an app he created every WhatsApp message he’d ever sent or received, and had the algorithm analyze his interactions with people including his wife and father

As he told a New Yorker reporter, “A lot of people don’t realize that, essentially, their WhatsApp history—across all their chats—is the diary they didn’t know they’d been writing.” But conducting wide-scale analyses of entire relationships like this also has the potential to launch us into sticky ethical territory
Many people think of text messages as ephemeral and private (despite evidence of the various ways we can be easily surveilled)

Our text threads with family and friends—the people we’re closest with—can therefore be quite honest, quite raw. “We had no idea when we started emailing and texting in the ’90s, 2000s, that these were records we’d be creating between us, which until that time were evanescent,” Jeff Hancock, a communication professor at Stanford University who studies AI-assisted conversation, told me. “Who knew that this would be a massive new thing,” he said, the fact that “private conversations between individuals would now have a record?” The idea that a person can so casually take the contents of their written communications—with or without other people’s consent—and ask an AI tool to ingest and analyze that data seems disquieting, if not downright dystopian
Hancock said that people’s use of chatbots to audit what we previously thought of as closed conversations will no doubt become more prevalent
This might feel like an intrusion, he acknowledged, but he could see net-positive benefits
Imagine a scenario, he suggested, in which “you’re like, Hey, look, I want to do right by my sister

I’ve been annoyed and frustrated with her .” A bot analyzing your text history might come up with the perfect thing to say the next time you call her. [ Read: The people who outsource emotional labor to AI ] Even so, Hancock noted that there are probably “lots of ways this will go wrong.” Consider chatbots that might not only analyze relationships as they evolve but also predict outcomes—which sounds a little Minority Report to me
And then there’s the question of accuracy: Chatbots are designed to serve, which means that they tend to communicate what they think people want to hear

Sometimes, an AI might “really unlock stuff” for a person, Hancock said. “But they’re sycophantic.” To be useful, the AI needs “to also take the perspective of the other person.” W hen I fed my text thread with Michael into ChatGPT, I found out—as I’d first hoped—a few things about my love life

I learned that I’m overly credulous when it comes to men’s stated intentions (“You can recognize that a man is unavailable, evasive, selfish, or inconsistent,” the bot said, “and nevertheless continue to treat his expressions of desire as evidence that something more meaningful might develop”) and that I’m looking for love in all the wrong places (“You sometimes recognize a man’s limitations but behave as though they are negotiable”)
Yet when the bot pivoted to spicy comments about Michael and me, it really drew me in

It said, for instance, that I have selective hearing and can be dismissive after he has offered well-meaning advice: “You ask him what he would do, but instead of seriously entertaining his answer, you almost instantly construct the case against it.” So, with Michael’s permission, I came up with a new query and pressed harder: “Please analyze this data set of text messages between Michael Wertheim and Anna Holmes, two friends, and craft a portrait of their friendship over the years.” I asked ChatGPT to look not just at what he and I had said to each other but at how we’d said it
After three minutes and 53 seconds, it told me that it had analyzed the entire archive—32,245 messages, from September 13, 2014, to June 25, 2026

It had a lot to say. “Their language with each other is extraordinarily unguarded,” it told me. “They discuss work humiliation, money, parents, family dysfunction, depression and anxiety, illness, aging, sex, dating apps, hookups, rejection, medications, bodily problems, loneliness and death.” And: “They can move in seconds from something serious to something ridiculous, from mortality to television, from depression to a bad date, from career anxiety to cat litter.” And: “Their friendship eventually acquires some of the infrastructure of family.” When I told a friend about this experiment and read her a few lines, though, she made a smart observation: It sounded like ChatGPT was presenting a pretty rosy picture of my part in the friendship
What if, she asked, I pushed it for a more candid assessment? So I asked it to be more brutally honest

In response, it conceded that it had been “somewhat restrained” in its analysis—and proceeded to give me some real talk, telling me, in bold type, “There are moments where I think you are plainly the harder person to be friends with .” It also shared a rather damning 10-point list of my transgressions, including a paragraph or two of elaboration with each item

Among its observations: “You can disappear into your own life and assume the friendship will simply survive it.” “You can center your interpretation of his experience over his own.” “You can be relentless when you think Michael is handling something badly.” “You can be absorbed enough in your own distress that Michael has to announce his needs explicitly.” Ouch
It stung because I’ve always worried that this is true; the bot’s assessment felt like a confirmation of that fear
It seemed to be saying: You’re easily distracted, myopic, over-opinionated, selfish

If I wanted to give myself some grace, I could remind myself that even though ChatGPT had a corpus of communication between us, this was still merely a snapshot of the relationship, not a complete picture
Surely the AI was blind to bits of nuance and didn’t always understand context or intent

title: Five Books That Would Make Great Movies
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture
Sometimes a book is engrossing enough to play out like a film in your mind—characters assemble in easy conversation, lush landscapes backdrop each scene
So I asked five Atlantic staffers: What is a book that you think would be a good fit for a movie adaptation? The Transit of Venus , by Shirley Hazzard Here’s a classic movie setup I’ll never tire of
A young, intrepid woman finds herself torn between two men: one dashing but boorish, the other sweet-natured but meek
If Bridget Jones has taught us anything, she’ll choose the wrong one—but watching her realize her error, and decide whether or not to correct it, is always thrilling (and agonizing)
This is the plot you’d get if you put Shirley Hazzard’s exquisite 1980 novel into a Shrinky Dinks machine
There are other storylines woven through it, but at its core, it’s both an unrequited-love story and a period piece: catnip for Hollywood
Caro Bell, a young Australian woman in 1950s England, chooses the rakish playwright Paul Ivory over the awkward scientist Ted Tice
Paul promptly breaks her heart, which sets her on a wandering path across decades and continents

Some creative makeup might be needed for the age progression, but one can easily envision the montages of far-flung destinations (Stockholm, Sydney); Hazzard’s lucid, dramatic dialogue wouldn’t need much tweaking, either. (The taglines practically write themselves: “All my weakness is distilled in you,” Caro tells Paul.) I won’t spoil the outcome, but know that it’s a tearjerker. — Sara Krolewski, deputy research chief *** The Secret History , by Donna Tartt Immediately after finishing The Secret History for the second time, I went to look up whether a movie adaptation had been made
I was disappointed to learn that not only is there no movie, but there have been multiple failed attempts to make one

Everything about this book makes it an excellent candidate for translation to film: the pacing; the characters; the bizarre, vivid plot (an imagination goes only so far in piecing together the bacchanal!)
At a liberal-arts college in New England, the unreliable narrator, Richard, meets a strange and secretive group of friends through their shared classics major
At first he is enamored with them, but he soon begins to realize that something about this group is very wrong
Unsettling rituals fueled by alcohol and drugs, irrevocable acts, and irredeemable lies all push Richard down a once-unimaginable path

I often find myself unimpressed with the adaptations of some of my favorite books, especially those with excellent prose—but in the right director’s hands, perhaps Richard’s blind obsession with this cast of characters could be shared with even more people. — Laney Crawley, editorial fellow *** Skippy Dies , by Paul Murray No one does tragicomedy quite like the Irish, and no Irish artist so masterfully combines the hilarious with the heartbreaking as Murray

He’s been feted for his most recent novel, The Bee Sting , but I prefer the earlier Skippy Dies , which focuses on a Dublin boarding school’s faculty and students—including, yes, Skippy, the unfortunate adolescent who fulfills the title’s promise in the opening pages

The nonlinear story explores the time before and after Skippy’s death; its abundant subplots feature morally suspect teachers, Skippy’s crush, a terrifying bully, and Skippy’s precocious, string-theory-obsessed roommate
All of this, to me, demands a big-screen treatment—something like Dead Poets Society as interpreted by Martin McDonagh
The Dublin depicted is an ominous, grim one, careening toward a post–Celtic Tiger recession and mired in ongoing Catholic Church scandals

And yet Skippy Dies manages to retain its sense of humor and a frenetic energy, hopping from character to character in a way that immerses readers in the messed-up but entertaining world of Seabrook College

Capturing even a fraction of the novel’s delirious style on-screen would be challenging, but I’d love to see someone try. — Dan Goff, copy editor *** The American Painter Emma Dial , by Samantha Peale I would love to see an adaptation of Samantha Peale’s 2009 novel, featuring an eponymous heroine who is a studio assistant to a very famous artist—which, in practice, means that she makes his paintings according to his instructions
The job is both stable and prestigious, and Emma enjoys it, but she’s well aware that it crowds out her personal artistic aspirations
Over the course of the book, which is full not only of art but of sex and status jockeying, she wrestles with her competing desires for a secure career and creative freedom
It’s a layered, fascinating portrait of ambition by Peale, who once worked as an assistant to Jeff Koons

Plus, all of the studio scenes, with their colossal canvases and vibrant colors, would look terrific on a big screen. — Lily Meyer, staff writer *** Moderation , by Elaine Castillo When Girlie Delmundo’s boss kisses her, she feels him everywhere—her lips, her neck, her fingertips
Which is odd, considering the two are not physically together, but making out in a fairground-themed simulation
Girlie, the protagonist, is a content moderator for a new virtual-reality experience
The novel, which moves between real life and cyberspace as Girlie does, benefits from Castillo’s incisive narration , which repeatedly evokes the five senses
Take Girlie’s maiden voyage into the augmented landscape: A “deafening chorus” seizes her first; a blinding sight—marble palaces under sunlight—follows
Shivers, from the fading snow underfoot, soon rack her avatar
At times, the descriptions are so vivid that they emphasize the lack of sensation involved in merely reading this book on your couch
But that’s what makes Moderation a perfect candidate for adaptation

<title>Prostate cancer testing now urged for men in their 50s and 60s – a lead author of the new screening guidelines explains why</title>
    <content type="html"><p><em>The American Cancer Society announced on Nov. 12, 2026, that it has <a href="https://pressroom.cancer.org/prostate-cancer-screening-guideline-update-2026">released major changes</a> to its prostate cancer screening guidelines to improve detection and treatment of the disease.</em></p>

<p><em>The Conversation asked <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=qgDmAewAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">Dr. Andrew Wolf</a>, a physician at the University of Virginia who was one of the <a href="https://doi.org/10.3322/caac.70112">lead authors of the new guidelines</a>, to walk readers through the changes and why they were made.</em></p>

<h2>What are the new screening recommendations?</h2>

<p>The biggest change is that we are making a <a href="https://pressroom.cancer.org/prostate-cancer-screening-guideline-update-2026">proactive recommendation to screen for prostate cancer</a>. Previously, we recommended that people talk with their healthcare provider to decide whether or not screening is right for them.</p>

<p>Our new recommendations <a href="https://doi.org/10.3322/caac.70112">vary by age and by a person’s risk</a> of developing prostate cancer.</p>

<p>For people at average risk of developing prostate cancer, we recommend they be screened with the <a href="https://www.cancer.gov/types/prostate/psa-fact-sheet">prostate-specific antigen, or PSA, blood test</a> every two years from age 50 through 69. PSA is a protein that prostate cells make. Cancer and other conditions can cause PSA levels to rise.</p>

<p>People at higher risk, including Black men and men with a strong family history of prostate cancer, should be screened annually from age 45 to 69. A strong family history means having a family member who was diagnosed with prostate cancer before age 65, or multiple family members diagnosed at any age. People with a single family member diagnosed at age 65 or older should be screened every two years from age 45 years to age 69 years.</p>

<p>For people ages 70 to 74, we recommend they talk with their healthcare provider about whether or not to continue screening. Because there is uncertainty about the benefit of screening for people in this age group, <a href="https://theconversation.com/prostate-cancer-treatment-is-not-always-the-best-option-a-cancer-researcher-walks-her-father-through-his-diagnosis-206975">decision-making around screening</a> depends on their personal preferences, overall health status and life expectancy. </p>

<p>For those over age 74, we recommend against prostate cancer screening. The potential harms of screening, such as more invasive follow-up tests and treatment, are likely to exceed the benefits for people in this age group. </p>

<p>Finally, we recommend against using a digital rectal exam to screen for prostate cancer, as it is <a href="https://doi.org/10.1370/afm.2205">less effective than the PSA test</a>. The digital rectal exam may still be helpful when further evaluating elevated PSA levels or symptoms related to the prostate gland.</p>

            </figcaption>

<h2>Why were the screening guidelines updated?</h2>

<p>The past decade has seen mounting evidence supporting the benefits of using the PSA blood test to screen for prostate cancer. </p>

<p>The ability of the PSA test to reduce the risk of <a href="https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2503223">death from prostate cancer</a> or of being <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eururo.2012.05.068">diagnosed with metastatic disease</a> are actually greater than researchers previously thought. </p>

<p>At the same time, there have been significant developments to reduce the potential harms associated with prostate cancer screening, including <a href="https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMcp2209151">false positive PSA test results</a> and diagnosis and treatment of prostate tumors that are <a href="https://doi.org/10.1097/JU.0000000000002758">unlikely to harm patients</a> in the long-term.</p>

<h2>Who is most at risk for prostate cancer?</h2>

<p>Black men have an approximately <a href="https://doi.org/10.3322/caac.70028">two-thirds higher risk</a> of developing prostate cancer compared with white men. They are also at greater risk for having more advanced disease at the time of diagnosis. These disparities are likely due to a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eururo.2022.03.007">combination of genetic, environmental, social and healthcare access factors</a>.</p>

<p>Men with a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1158/1078-0432.CCR-18-0370">family history of prostate cancer</a> in a close relative – such as a parent, sibling or child – are also at elevated risk. </p>

<p>There are also a number of genetic mutations, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41585-022-00680-4">such as <em>BRCA2</em></a>, that confer significantly elevated risk of prostate cancer. Though screening recommendations for these cases are beyond the scope of our guideline, several professional medical organizations, including the <a href="https://doi.org/10.6004/jnccn.2026.0007">National Comprehensive Cancer Network</a> and the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1097/JU.0000000000003491">American Urological Association</a>, have issued recommendations for screening people with these high-risk mutations. </p>

<h2>Why has the PSA test been so controversial?</h2>

<p>For years, clinicians believed that the benefits of PSA screening were uncertain and didn’t necessarily outweigh the potential harms. This stance was in part because of the results of two large prostate cancer screening trials that were published in 2009. One, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa0810696">a U.S. study</a>, found no benefit to screening; the other, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa0810084">a European study</a>, found only a relatively small benefit. </p>

<p>However, it later became clear that the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMc1515131">U.S. study was seriously flawed</a> in such a way that it couldn’t have shown a benefit: Almost 90% of the men in the control group – that is, the group that wasn’t supposed to get screened – actually did get screened, and many of the men with abnormal PSA levels didn’t follow-up. </p>

<p>Conversely, most of the men in the European study who were randomized to standard care – no testing – instead of screening did not, in fact, get a PSA test, so it was more of a true comparison of the effect of screening versus not screening. </p>

<p>After researchers <a href="https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2503223">followed patients for over two decades</a> in the European study, the effects of screening became clear: Screening reduced the risk of dying from prostate cancer by 13%. And about 500 men needed to be screened to avert one death from prostate cancer. </p>

<p>This may not sound very impressive, but it’s comparable to other routinely offered cancer screening tests, such as <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s10549-023-07124-6">mammography for breast cancer</a>. And the proportion of people needing to be screened to save a life would be significantly lower if extrapolated to a lifetime of screening starting at age 45 or 50, rather than the average number of two screenings that men received in the study.</p>

<h2>Why are there differences in guidelines?</h2>

<p>The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force also has its own prostate cancer screening guidelines. The task force’s guidelines currently recommend that clinicians not screen for prostate cancer unless the patient indicates a preference to proceed. At the time of the task force’s <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2018.3710">last update in 2018</a>, it determined that the potential benefits and harms of screening were too closely balanced to recommend screening.</p>

<p>The task force has been <a href="https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/draft-update-summary/prostate-cancer-screening-adults">in the process of updating</a> those guidelines over the past several years. It is possible that their update will more closely align with that of the American Cancer Society.</p>

<p>I do think we have both sufficient evidence of benefit and sufficient reduction of the risks to now proactively recommend screening. Where the two guidelines do align is that both recommend that patients be informed of the benefits, risks and limitations of prostate cancer screening so they know what they’re getting into. </p>

<p>It is likely that our new screening recommendations will be covered by most insurers. However, patients may have out-of-pocket costs for further testing their doctor orders as a result of an abnormal PSA level.</p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>What would you say to people hesitant about screening?</h2>

<p>Even though the benefits far outweigh the risks, there may be legitimate reasons why some people may not wish to undergo screening.</p>

<p>Some people might want to avoid the possibility of needing to get a <a href="https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/prostate-cancer/detection-diagnosis-staging/how-diagnosed.html">prostate biopsy</a>, which is how clinicians diagnose prostate cancer if a patient has an elevated PSA and an abnormal follow-up MRI scan or biomarker test. Prostate biopsies are uncomfortable, and they may cause some bleeding or occasionally an infection. </p>

<p>Some people may want to avoid the possibility of needing to <a href="https://theconversation.com/prostate-cancer-treatment-is-not-always-the-best-option-a-cancer-researcher-walks-her-father-through-his-diagnosis-206975">undergo active surveillance</a> if they discover they have a tumor that <a href="https://theconversation.com/what-does-it-mean-for-bidens-prostate-cancer-to-be-aggressive-a-urologic-surgeon-explains-257100">isn’t growing aggressively</a>. Active surveillance involves periodic biopsies, MRI scans or both, which can be inconvenient and anxiety-provoking. </p>

<p>Some people may want to avoid the potential side effects of <a href="https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/prostate-cancer/treating.html">treating early-stage prostate cancer</a> with surgery or radiation, which can cause sexual, urinary and bowel problems.</p>

<p>Forgoing screening, however, also means forgoing the opportunity to find cancer at its earliest stages, when the chance for a cure is very high.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/296645/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: Men weren’t always “bad at friendship”
excerpt: Summer's Eve (1893) by Norwegian painter Halfdan Egedius. | Heritage Art/Heritage Images via Getty Images The headlines may be dominated by artificial intellige
body: Summer's Eve (1893) by Norwegian painter Halfdan Egedius. | Heritage Art/Heritage Images via Getty Images The headlines may be dominated by artificial intelligence and electoral politics, but beneath it all, another debate constantly simmers, forever threatening to erupt
I write, of course, of the great male friendship debate

On one side: writers, journalists, and academics who fret over rising male loneliness , the emotional impact of friendless men on their partners , and the threat to society posed by atomized and isolated fellas
On the other: those who defend male friendships built around shared activities rather than heart-to-hearts
These arguments often talk past each other

But the historian Tiffany Watt Smith offered me a way to think differently about both: that the gender roles undergirding the conversation are not nearly as fixed as they seem. “I can definitely tell you that men in the past had much more intimate and romantic and involved friendships than we see today, for sure,” said Smith, who has published a number of books on the histories of friendship and emotions . “The idea that women are the kind of great experts in friendship is a really modern idea.” I talked with Smith about Aristotle’s idea of the “perfect” friendship (it has to be between two dudes), how gendered notions of friendship inverted in the 19th century, and what men seeking deeper emotional connection from their buddies can learn from the past
You can hear that conversation and and more on the latest episode of Explain It to Me , Vox’s weekly call-in podcast
Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Smith, edited for length and clarity
You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , or wherever you get your podcasts
If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545

How do male friendships today compare to those of the past? For thousands of years, it was really men who were considered the great experts in knowing how to form the highest kinds of friendships and the most intimate kind of bonds
And their friendships were considered the most meaningful and enduring and deep kind of friendships
If you look back at David and Jonathan in the Bible or Achilles and Patroclus in the Iliad , you see these very dynamic, committed male friendships
When we look at the writings of Aristotle in the fourth-century BC, he’s talking about the deepest kind of friendship
And this is between two men who he sees as soulmates
And he does say that there are other kinds of friendship, which are lesser friendships
He says you might make friends because it’s kind of convenient or because you enjoy doing the same kinds of things, or maybe you’re trying to help each other out
There’s a kind of quid pro quo-type of friendship
So he does see these kinds of friendship all around him
And he says women do those kinds of friendships

One of the most famous pieces of writing about friendship ever is Michel de Montaigne’s essay “On Friendship.” Montaigne was a 16th-century essayist and lawyer, and he had this very, very close and committed friendship with another writer called La Boétie

And then after La Boétie died very unexpectedly, Montaigne wrote about their friendship and he said they had this kind of ideal friendship, the kind that Aristotle wrote about, this meeting of souls, and that this was rare and extraordinary
He said, “Men can have these kinds of friendships.” But he very explicitly said, “Women are just incapable of having this kind of perfect friendship
They don’t have the kind of emotional stamina
Their souls aren’t strong enough, essentially, to withstand the complexities and difficulties of friendship.” So it’s a complete inversion from what we see today
You used this word when you started: romantic

What did you mean by that? Was the Aristotelian conception of a perfect male friendship, was there a kind of romantic element in the way that we use the word romance? Historians call this style of friendship “romantic friendship.” It doesn’t necessarily mean that they were having a physically active relationship or that they were having sex
They did see themselves as a partnership, and some of these male friends talked about themselves as married
This was a marriage of soul. “Friendship is something that we have to negotiate on an individual basis

Each friendship is completely singular and we have to work out its rules.” There’s a very important tombstone in Christ’s College in Cambridge, which commemorates these two doctors in the 16th century who basically lived their whole lives together
They traveled together, they did their research together and so on
And when they died, they were buried together
And the tomb does look like a conventional tomb between a husband and wife
Now, we don’t know anything about their relationship in practice

I mean, the thing that really matters is the fact that this friendship, because it was commemorated as a friendship, the fact that it could be commemorated so vividly and publicly in such an extravagant way shows us that this is a culture that accepts and idealizes this kind of male friendship
So how do we get from there to here? Beginning in the 18th century and certainly by the 19th century, there’s a series of things that happen
One is that we get a distinction between the public space of the workplaces, cities are expanding, offices start to exist

The male sphere is fashioned as one of being in public, being a more rational sphere, and the female sphere starts to be connected with the home and intimacy and emotion.  Those ideas have been kind of floating around for a while, but they start to get really consolidated in the 19th century

And at the same time, a new ideal of femininity starts to emerge and it becomes a real sort of middle-class aspirational goal for women that they have very close friendships, almost as evidence that they can do all of these things
Young girls in this era are taught a very particular style of friendship, which is, again, it’s very romantic

title: Why do people keep dumping buckets of fish into Montana’s lakes?
excerpt: An angler displays a lake trout, considered an invasive species, that they caught on Lake McDonald in Glacier National Park in Montana on October 18, 2023. | Jo
body: An angler displays a lake trout, considered an invasive species, that they caught on Lake McDonald in Glacier National Park in Montana on October 18, 2023. | Josh Edelson/AFP via Getty Images On a summer day in 1992, a man dumped a cooler full of a fish called yellow perch into Lake Mary Ronan, in northwest Montana.  We know this because two teenagers saw him do it; they wrote down his license plate number and called in a tip to the Montana Fish, Wildlife, and Parks department (FWP), which immediately dispatched biologists to capture and kill the perch with nets and poison.  The teenagers got a reward of $500 each for their efforts, while the man was charged with illegally introducing non-native fish into the lake, slapped with a small fine, and sent on his way

The law changed soon after: Now, intentionally introducing a non-native, invasive species to Montana’s waters is a felony punishable by as long as two years in prison or a fine of up to $25,000, or both.  Why I wrote about this I visited Flathead Lake Biological Station in October, and while I was there I heard from a biologist about this strange, totally avoidable, invisible catastrophe in the making
I was absolutely fascinated — as I looked at the lake, I hardly believed it could lose its signature clarity because of a bucketful of fish — and decided I had no choice but to open this can of worms
But the perch? The yellow perch — at least two of them — survived, multiplied, and quickly went on to wreak havoc
They established dominance in the lake, wiping out its population of a native fish called the Westslope Cutthroat trout and causing other ecosystem disruptions
This hasn’t only happened here: Montana is filled with thousands of beautiful alpine lakes and rivers, nestled in the sort of rugged territory that sold people on the idea of the West

Yet, across the state, without permission, people keep dumping non-native fish into them.  The reason is simple: The introduced fish, according to some anglers, are more fun to fish than the stuff that’s already swimming around in Montana’s waters

But this guerrilla ecology — or “ bucket biology ” as some call it — risks upending delicate, longstanding ecosystems, harming not only native fish, but also animals that depend on them, like bald eagles, bears, and otters
It could turn Montana’s pristine waters into murky messes that also require millions of dollars in cleanup and additional maintenance every year.  And it’s not just a problem in Montana
Across the country, states are trying to stop people from filling lakes with fish that don’t belong

It’s a high-stakes issue with ramifications that can reach far beyond the underwater neighborhood of a single lake; efforts to stop illegal fish-dumping have now spawned everything from high-dollar bounties and dedicated fish forensics.  “A decision made by one person can affect an entire interconnected ecosystem,” said Craig Barfoot, Fisheries Program Manager for the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes (CSKT), which is based on the Flathead Reservation in northwestern Montana and oversees some of the most pristine aquatic habitats in the state. “It’s like an act of arson.” The power of a bucket Flathead Lake, about an hour’s drive south of Glacier National Park, is the sort of place postcards were made for

The 27-mile-long lake, half within the Flathead Reservation (and overseen by the tribes) and half managed by the state, is one of the cleanest, clearest lakes in the populated world —  a survey last year found that the lake is clear down to about 36 feet — which draws all sorts of creatures to its shore

During a two-day visit in October, I saw a black bear ambling along the shore and a bald eagle sitting in a tree, tearing into a fish it had scooped out of the water.  This massive glacial lake “was ice about 15,000 years ago,” said Tom Bansak, associate director of the Flathead Lake Bio Station, a research station in the lake that’s run by the University of Montana. “Before western contact, there were maybe eight to 10 species of fish in the lake, which is not very many for a lake of its size.”  That changed starting in the late 1800s, when wildlife managers at the federal and state levels decided to start stocking lakes around the country with fish that were raised in hatcheries and released into the water for recreational fishing

For decades, states mostly made stocking decisions based not on local ecologies but rather on the kinds of fish people wanted to catch, filling them with nonnative fish like trout, bass, walleye, and pike

If you live in the United States, there’s a good chance the closest popular fishing spot is filled with stocked fish; at Flathead Lake, wildlife managers introduced around 30 different kinds of non-native fish, of which about a dozen established spawning populations, and today non-native fish outnumber native ones.  Eventually, state wildlife agencies began to realize that this sort of recreation-driven stocking can harm local ecosystems: In the 1970s, for example, Montana decided to stop stocking non-native fish in most of its streams and rivers
It still stocks plenty of fish , though, including a few non-native species, in some of its lakes and reservoirs, as do most other states.  For some people, however, that’s not enough

Some anglers believe the fish native to Montana, like bull trout, cutthroat trout, and sturgeon, just aren’t as fun to catch or as tasty to eat as, say, northern pike and walleye — both of which have been illegally introduced to the state’s waters in recent years

It can take as little as a bucketful of fish to alter the population of an entire lake, which means that if someone is bored of the fishing options at their local lake, they could unilaterally decide to spice things up with little risk of getting caught

Despite nonnative fish introductions now being a felony in Montana (and at least four other states), not a single person has been charged, let alone convicted there; that man the two teens saw at Lake Mary Ronan more than 30 years ago is the only person to have ever even been reported.  “People are mad at us, and they vocally say it.” Sam Bourret, FWP Fisheries biologist But fish and wildlife officials know it’s still happening because they keep finding non-native fish in the state’s waterways, and the most likely way they got there is by someone illegally dumping them in.  “They’re obviously avid anglers, and we probably know them,” said Sam Bourret, a fisheries biologist at FWP based near Flathead Lake

Investigating illegal fish introductions is Bourret’s speciality: The Great Falls Tribune called him the “ fish detective ” for pioneering a forensic technique that looks at chemical clues inside otoliths , fishes’ stone-like ear bones, to figure out where they might have come from

He’s also used data modeling based on conditions like elevation and fishing pressure to figure out which lakes might be most vulnerable to future fish introductions, which could help steer resources towards them and stop would-be bucket biologists

From his time on the job, which has included many firsthand interactions with anglers, he can tell many of them are irked that they can’t stock the fish they want wherever they want them. “I do think some of these people are spiteful in their desire to move fish around,” Bourret said. “People are mad at us, and they vocally say it.” Sometimes the culprit is less intentional

Non-native fish that are kept in ponds on private property (which technically require permits to build and stock but often slip by under the radar) can get into nearby rivers or lakes if the pond overflows during a storm, or by being picked up by a bird and then dropped into another waterbody

Earlier this year, FWP biologists on Bourret’s team removed 4,000 goldfish from a pond at a hotel on the edge of Montana’s Thompson River; the pond had been an attraction for families visiting the hotel with small children, who liked to scoop fish out of the water with nets

But goldfish can be disastrous for freshwater ecosystems , and the FWP wanted to be sure they wouldn’t slip into the adjacent river — and from there into a nearby lake.  But they often don’t get so far ahead of a potential problem. “Introduced fish probably go undetected often,” Bourret said. “We usually find out about them through a needle in a haystack catch

Once a population sets up in a lake, it’s already way too late.”  Fish-shaped dominoes Monitoring species in the underwater realm of rivers, lakes, and streams is vastly more challenging than it is on land. “It’s a lot more obvious when a terrestrial animal doesn’t belong,” says Andrew Gilham, Fisheries Management Bureau Chief at FWP. “If you see a zebra in Montana, you’d probably think it’s weird

But if people see a brown trout, which is from Europe, it just doesn’t register in the same way.”  And that may even play into the general public’s understanding of just how much impact a few fish can have. “Some of it may just be that they don’t really understand the consequences that can follow illegal introductions,” he said.  Aquatic ecosystems are delicate balances, and in a healthy lake the populations of fish, predators, and small organisms like zooplankton and phytoplankton typically exist in a hard-won equilibrium

To simplify greatly, there are usually enough zooplankton to eat phytoplankton and prevent algal blooms, enough zooplankton-eating fish to prevent the zooplankton from eating all the phytoplankton, and enough predators to keep those zooplankton-eating fish in check — but not so many that the smaller fish get wiped out.  “If you see a zebra in Montana, you’d probably think it’s weird

But if people see a brown trout, which is from Europe, it just doesn’t register in the same way.” Andrew Gilham, Montana Fish, Wildlife, and Parks Bucket biology, especially with voracious carnivores like pike, is a bit like tossing a fish-shaped grenade into the lake

If the newcomers establish a spawning population, they can compete for resources with the native fish or eat them directly, eventually causing something called a trophic cascade: a domino-like series of events that can upend an entire ecosystem
What happens to fish in a lake can have huge effects on the creatures outside of it, too
In the Yellowstone region, Yellowstone Lake had long been home to a native fish species called the cutthroat trout

These fish would make long, winding spawning migrations through the Yellowstone lake and river system, where some four mammal species and 16 bird species — bears, otters, eagles, and pelicans, among others — would pluck them out of the water for meals

The migrating cutthroat were also important vectors for nutrients, which came from the fish’s poop and were important food sources for plants and algae growing in and along the waterways.  But then, in the 1990s, a non-native species arrived (likely through an illegal introduction): lake trout
Lake trout eat cutthroat, and without any predators of their own, they could feast on the smaller fish without anything to stop them

Once the lake trout appeared in Yellowstone Lake, they decimated cutthroat populations; according to a report from the National Park Service , by 1998, there were some 125,000 lake trout in the lake, and they ate somewhere between 3 and 4 million cutthroat that year.  Zooplankton in the lake, which the cutthroat used to eat, had a population boom, which led to a decline in phytoplankton

And the lake trout just stayed in the lake rather than migrating through the rivers and streams like the cutthroat did, which not only robbed those waters of the additional nutrients they brought, but also took a of a high-impact food source away from bears, otters, and birds

Bear and otter activity alongside the streams declined; while bears are opportunistic feeders and likely found another food source, the otters probably had a harder time finding something to supplement their diets

Bald eagle nests saw a sharp decline in their success rates after cutthroat disappeared, and osprey nest counts fell from 60 in 2001 to 3-5 from 2008-2015.  “We don’t want to just be moving things around willy-nilly,” said Niall Clancy , director of the Fisheries Lab at Salish Kootenai College. “Because one thing we learned is that we are bad at predicting the impacts — and there’s a good chance that something will go wrong that we didn’t think of.” And, Clancy added, these sorts of introductions can cause financial cascades alongside trophic ones: FWP now spends millions of dollars each year to reduce invasive fish populations in the state’s lakes and boost native fish populations through hatchery programs

This, in turn, diverts money away from other programs.   Can the buckets be stopped?  Stopping illegal fish introductions is a nearly impossible task; catching someone red-handed would require vigilantly monitoring thousands and thousands of miles of shoreline in Montana

title: National ground stop response highlights critical errors in public reassurance – saying ‘nothing nefarious’ did the opposite of quelling public concern

<title>National ground stop response highlights critical errors in public reassurance – saying ‘nothing nefarious’ did the opposite of quelling public concern</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771985/original/file-20261114-64-80wrmw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5034%2C3355&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">An information board at the Chicago O&#39;Hare International Airport on Nov.13, 2026, after the Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop on all departing flights.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/view-of-an-information-board-at-the-chicago-ohare-news-photo/2304526823?phrase=ground%20stop&amp;adppopup=true">Jacek Boczarski/Anadolu via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p><em><a href="https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/11/14/us/faa-nationwide-ground-stop-flights">Thousands of travelers were stranded</a> on Nov. 13, 2026, when the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all domestic flights in the U.S. because of what they said were <a href="https://www.kake.com/news/national/you-will-have-more-of-these-unless-system-upgraded-duffy-says-of-outage-that-led/article_4cbc8ca8-cbe2-4119-af1e-6b0de1def505.html">failures in decades-old air traffic communications systems</a>. <a href="https://sc.edu/study/colleges_schools/cic/faculty-staff/bowen_shannon.php">Crisis communications expert Shannon A. Bowen</a>, a scholar at the University of South Carolina’s College of Information and Communications, spoke with The Conversation’s Politics and Legal Affairs Editor, Naomi Schalit, about how the Trump administration handled the first day of the crisis.</em></p>

<p><em>This interview has been edited for length and clarity.</em></p>

<hr>

<p><strong>Is there a first principle in crisis communications?</strong></p>

<p>The first principle would be to react quickly and react with accuracy, react with everything you know at the moment, truthfully, but always react quickly. Because if you delay until you gather information, a vacuum will ensue. Information fills that vacuum that may not be accurate. And so that’s the enemy of accurate crisis communication, but you want to always speak quickly and be the most authoritative and definitive source, even if very little information is known. </p>

<p><strong>What did we see on the day of the ground stop?</strong> </p>

<p>A crisis unfolded and to the administration’s credit, <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Yuwrrs8MBPc">they did react very quickly</a>, in a way that offered the information that was known at the time, even though not a lot was known about why the ground stop was issued until later. </p>

<p><strong>You’re speaking about the <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Yuwrrs8MBPc">short press conference that afternoon</a> with Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin?</strong></p>

<p>He did keep saying that <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YBLQm2dDl6Y">nothing nefarious was at hand</a>. And for a crisis communication scholar, <a href="https://www.researchgate.net/publication/397432409_Principles_of_Effective_Crisis_Communication">you would not want to introduce the idea</a> that something nefarious was at hand, unless, indeed, something nefarious was at hand. So by the very act of introducing this concept and this idea, I think the talking point, “Nothing nefarious,” then went across multiple networks, and it became the center of a controversy rather than quelling a controversy. </p>

<p>By saying nothing nefarious is at hand, that indeed confirmed something nefarious was at hand, even if the nefariousness was only the mismanagement of the air traffic control systems routers that they claimed caused the problem. By introducing this idea, I believe it did bring to mind that there may be other state actors behind whatever happened, that it could be a cyber attack. It would have been better to say, “We have evidence that this was not a cyber attack but a hardware failure.” </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/AEvP0w4Pk98?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin tells reporters that there was no indication of ‘nefarious’ activity causing the nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13, 2026.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p><strong>How did the later press conference with Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy go from your perspective as an expert on crisis communications?</strong> </p>

<p>They handled the questions that they received correctly. They told us as much information as they knew. </p>

<p>However, they did seem to downplay the extent of this crisis, because we have to remember the traveling public is not just people trying to get to business meetings. </p>

<p>We had football teams stranded. Now <a href="https://www.ksnblocal4.com/2026/11/13/sudden-faa-ground-stop-strands-teams-throws-upcoming-sports-weekend-into-chaos/">football Saturday</a>, all over the SEC, has been disrupted. And there’s probably disruption in other areas of the country, but to us in the South, <a href="https://time.com/5349530/paul-finebaum-football/">SEC football is almost a religious experience on Saturday</a>. Luckily, <a href="https://www.thestate.com/sports/college/university-of-south-carolina/usc-womens-basketball/article318071121.html">the University of South Carolina football team had already flown out</a>. But our marching band was stuck in this crisis, and so we have a lot of ripple effects from something like this happening, and it definitely says to me that this was an emergency situation. It wasn’t simply a crisis, it was an actual emergency of impending disaster-level scale. </p>

<p>If it were simply routers being overloaded, as we’ve been told, why wouldn’t they already know this situation and restart those routers the night before or over Friday night after most of the traveling public is out of the air? </p>

<p><strong>What was Mullin’s and Duffy’s job when they got out there? What did they need to do?</strong></p>

<p>To inform the public about the danger, why this happened, the extent of the problem, and what they’re doing to remediate the problem. <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/13/faa-orders-nationwide-grounding-of-passenger-planes-01166043">We keep hearing that they’re asking for US$30 billion</a> and more to repair the whole infrastructure for the air traffic control system, which is great, but what are they doing right now? </p>

<p>How do we know that flights in the air, right this minute, are any safer than the ones yesterday, a minute before the ground stop? Do we have that information? I don’t feel confident that they addressed that question appropriately. I don’t think that the traveling public entirely feels safe at this point or adequately informed that they will arrive at their destination. </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/Mh2q-y0wIu8?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Press conference with Markwayne Mullin and Sean Duffy on Nov. 13, 2026.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p><strong>They introduced <a href="https://rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/donald-trump-press-briefing-markwayne-mullin-sean-duffy-faa-ground-stop-november-13-2026/">politics into the press conference</a> as well, didn’t they?</strong> </p>

<p>It’s something that they have the prerogative to do. They are <a href="https://www.c-span.org/event/news-conference/cabinet-officials-brief-on-nationwide-ground-stop/449525">both political appointees and members of the cabinet</a>. So I understand that aspect, but I really wish they had addressed the traveling public’s concerns more overtly before making it political, that they need more money to fix this. We know they need more money to fix it, and I’m sure the American taxpayers are aware of the problem and willing to fund those corrections. But the more expedient issues would be, what about <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/aerospace-defense/thousands-us-flights-canceled-delayed-air-travel-system-recovers-shutdown-2026-11-14/">all these people who were stuck in airports</a>?</p>

<p><strong>Were there warning signs for this crisis?</strong> </p>

<p>I believe there were. We had <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/us/2023-ground-stop-faa-pilot-warning-system.html">another ground stop about three years ago</a>, due to air traffic control problems, and that is <a href="https://doi.org/10.4135/9781452275956.n139">what we call in crisis communications a “prodrome</a>,” a warning sign of larger impending problems. When you see these types of warning signs, it really gives us a reason to think it’s going to get worse. </p>

<p><strong>Duffy did say on Nov. 13 that, because of the condition of the air traffic infrastructure, “<a href="https://www.kake.com/news/national/you-will-have-more-of-these-unless-system-upgraded-duffy-says-of-outage-that-led/article_4cbc8ca8-cbe2-4119-af1e-6b0de1def505.html">you will have more</a>” ground stoppages. If you had a piece of advice for the administration regarding their future communications, what would you tell them?</strong></p>

<p>I would say to communicate in advance as much as possible, so if you’re even considering a ground stop, it may be a good idea to put out a public notice so that people don’t go to the airport on a vacation flight, maybe they delay that for a week or two. It might also be a good idea to speak with the airline industry representatives and say, “Here’s what we’re thinking. Can you work with us? How can we make this better for the traveling public?” Also, if 17 of 22 routers were malfunctioning, could we have had a partial ground stop at only the affected airports, rather than a nationwide stop?</p>

<p><strong>My silly last question: Do crisis communications experts have any theories about Friday the 13th?</strong> </p>

<p>We consider it more of a superstition, but I have noticed that there does tend to be a lot of activity on Friday the 13th. It might be placebo effect, it might be because we expect something bad to happen and we’re looking for it. But that day does seem to always have some type of activity. This is also when organizations release bad news, oftentimes, they say, “Let’s hold it until Friday the 13th, because bad news is expected.” People will assume, on Friday the 13th, that negative things are going to come out, so the shock value won’t be as much.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/296663/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
<p class="fine-print"><em><span>Shannon A. Bowen received funding in 2022-2023 from The National Science Foundation as PI on a grant studying disaster management.</span></em></p></content>
