title: Preventing campus sexual assault could start in kindergarten
excerpt: The campus of Cornell University on September 30, soon after the New York attorney general announced a review of the school’s handling of assault allegations. |
body: The campus of Cornell University on September 30, soon after the New York attorney general announced a review of the school’s handling of assault allegations. | Spencer Platt/Getty Images In the weeks since Jane Doe alleged she was gang-raped at a Cornell University fraternity party in 2024, the plague of campus sexual assault has once again become the topic of a heated national debate
Those discussions inevitably land on familiar solutions
Experts, pundits, and parents argue for stricter criminal laws and a more transparent and punitive Title IX campus adjudicatory process

But these solutions have been tried in the past and not proven effective: Campus climate surveys show persistently high rates of assault, and Cornell’s own data show that reported incidents rose from 23 percent to 35 percent between 2023 and 2025
It’s increasingly clear that to make meaningful progress requires a focus on prevention — not just punishment

Anyone horrified by the Cornell fraternity text thread published by the New York Times would agree that enforcement is only part of the story, and a fuller solution would begin with raising young people who don’t think it is remotely okay to treat each other’s bodies and emotions this way
There is a group of scholars and advocates across the country who are working on one surprisingly effective policy that might get us closer to that goal: comprehensive sex education

But not sex ed as it’s currently taught in most American public schools — a haphazard set of state programs, often deeply political, which often stress abstinence over how to be in healthy sexual relationships with other people

This other version, known as comprehensive sex ed and currently required in just seven states , takes a holistic approach with focus on how to refuse unwanted sexual advances, establish clear boundaries, and have intimate relationships based on open communication and mutual desire, not force, coercion, or extreme intoxication.  An important step in the prevention of sexual assault is making comprehensive sex ed more common in American schools, and, in the states that do, making that education start earlier and comply with the National Sex Education Standards

Evidence suggests that this kind of instruction can reduce sexual violence.  Giving young people information about contraception and how to avoid STIs is an essential part of sex ed, but it isn’t enough

Far too many of our children head off to college without the interpersonal skills required to have healthy relationships involving physical intimacy, which are critical to their psychological development into caring and fulfilled adults.  The consequences can be devastating, and I see them firsthand
I am a law professor who runs a clinical program at the University of San Francisco that trains second- and third-year law students by having them litigate real cases under close supervision
Since 2018, we have been representing Title IX clients — the accusers and those they accuse — at colleges and universities all over the United States
In every case, every time, the end result is the same: pain, heartbreak, and ruined lives
The legal “resolution” is almost beside the point.  The allegations in the Cornell case are at the extreme end of the spectrum
In nearly all of the cases we handle, there is no malicious intent or casual cruelty
Instead, there are two young people who are inexperienced, hesitant to convey their real feelings, and bad at reading nonverbal cues
They drink excessively and use drugs to overcome their awkwardness and insecurity, which only makes the poor communication worse
My colleague and I joke bleakly that we are in the wrong business
What we really need to be doing is going to secondary schools and preaching the value of comprehensive sex ed to tweens and teens to stop these assaults from happening in the first place

Recently, I interviewed Jennifer Hirsch, who is a professor at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and the co-author with Princeton sociologist Shamus Khan of the book Sexual Citizens , which synthesizes the findings of a five-year study of campus sexual assault that surveyed 2,000 students attending Columbia and Barnard.  “Thinking ambitiously about prevention requires that we get some more tools in the toolbox.” Jennifer Hirsch, Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health Sex education needs to start in kindergarten, she said, by teaching children to respect the bodies of their classmates by keeping their hands to themselves and refraining from playground activities like chasing down a classmate trying to kiss them

In higher grades, she explained, the instruction should change to become more age-appropriate, gradually adding topics relating to sexual health for tweens and teens “to teach the things you need to know, to grow into being a person who can have sex without hurting other people or yourself.” Currently, only Washington and Oregon start this early. (A few other states begin in first grade.) While it is true that many colleges and universities have mandatory trainings for students that involve learning about consent, bystander intervention, and how intoxication is a risk factor for sexual assault, it is too little, too late

By then, Hirsch said, “there is a non-trivial possibility that they’ve already experienced sexual violence or perpetrated sexual violence.” She compared it to “starting with calculus when they’ve never done arithmetic.” The need for such education is even more urgent today when kids snap and text instead of talk face-to-face as they are fed a diet of toxic social media messages and violent pornography that tells them what women want is to be dominated, degraded, and objectified

Gen Z in particular is in desperate need of a sexual education that is designed to dispel the fear, shame, and ignorance most young people feel around this topic and replace it with candid instruction on how to set boundaries, read cues, and treat intimate partners — whether it is a long-term relationship or a casual hook-up — with a basic modicum of respect and care.  Study after study has shown that there is widespread bipartisan support for having sex ed incorporated into secondary school instruction that teaches students the skills they need to have safe and healthy sexual relationships
Comprehensive sex education holds promise in combatting sexual assault, although the data is limited

A 2016 survey of more than 1,600 college students led by John Santelli, who is also a professor at Columbia’s Mailman School (and Hirsch’s spouse) found that when high schoolers received comprehensive sex education, it lowered their risk of sexual assault in college
Instruction stressing abstinence or how to avoid unwanted pregnancies and STIs did not.  This makes intuitive sense
If a young person learns early on how to extricate themselves from a sexual encounter that has turned uncomfortable or scary, they will be more likely to leave before an assault happens

If he or she is taught that other people’s bodies are not theirs for the taking, they will be less likely to violate them and instead ask for clarity whenever there is ambiguity about consent.  Still most schools shy away from such instruction. “It is better to tell kids that rape is bad than to say nothing,” but to stop there and hope for the best is not effective, Hirsch told me. “Thinking ambitiously about prevention requires that we get some more tools in the toolbox.”  But comprehensive sex ed, despite its popularity, has for decades been blocked by a minority of loud opposition, often motivated by religious beliefs , in states that consider adopting it
Since 2017 , New York state lawmakers have advocated for a law mandating comprehensive sex ed for students in grades K-12
Every year, Hirsch told me, it dies in committee

At the federal level, the Trump administration has eliminated most of the federal grant money for sex ed that isn’t abstinence-only even though the research has shown that telling kids to “just say no” to sex has no impact on their behavior
Suspension, expulsion, even criminal prosecution are not the solutions

They are the inadequate answers on offer by the adults in the room, who are trained only to react once the problem has become too big and ugly to ignore in any particular case before bracing for the next one
Reducing the accused to monsters and the accuser to a pitiable victim reinfects the wound, it does nothing to heal it

Wringing one’s hands and asking why, a generation later nothing has changed, virtually guarantees that nothing ever will.  If we really want to combat the plague of sexual assault on campus, we need to vaccinate our children in the same way we would against a lethal virus
Comprehensive sex ed is the best place to start.

title: “A rich message, but a poor campaign”: How Scott Colom beat the odds in Mississippi
excerpt: Bennie Thompson (D-MS) speaks during a victory celebration for Mississippi Sen.-elect Scott Colom at Tougaloo College in Tougaloo, Mississippi, on November 11,
body: Bennie Thompson (D-MS) speaks during a victory celebration for Mississippi Sen.-elect Scott Colom at Tougaloo College in Tougaloo, Mississippi, on November 11, 2026. | Aron Smith/Jackson State University via Getty Images On Wednesday, Mississippi’s Senate race was officially called for Democrat Scott Colom, who will become the first Black person to represent the state in the US Senate since Reconstruction, more than 140 years ago
Colom’s win is a stunning, historic upset — and for many Black Democrats, like Rep
Bennie Thompson, it’s been a long time coming
Thompson, who also won his race last week, has represented Mississippi’s majority-Black Second Congressional District since 1993

Over the years, the 78-year-old lawmaker has frequently invoked the story of his father, who was never able to cast a vote because of racist Jim Crow laws that enforced segregation until the mid-1960s

I sat down with Thompson for Today, Explained to talk about Colom’s run for Senate, how he won, what it means for Thompson personally.  Below is an excerpt of our conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify
Your dad was never able to cast a vote during his lifetime because of Jim Crow laws
And I wonder, growing up in Mississippi, what did you learn about who was allowed to participate in democracy? You were a second-class citizen
That means you could go to school, but you couldn’t go to school with the white kids
Or the one swimming pool in town was for white kids, and the Black kids had to swim in the creeks or the ponds around the community
My mama and daddy paid taxes, but they weren’t allowed to vote
My uncle fought in World War II; defended democracy all over the world, but when he came back home, he had to ride a segregated train behind the white German prisoners
Jesus.  So you had the white soldiers, the white German prisoners, and the Black soldiers

It was something that we grew up with.  When you were young, I wonder, did you associate the right to vote with the ability to change things? Like, if we get to cast a ballot, then we get to fix this mess?  The best thing that I can say is I went to Tougaloo College [near Jackson, Mississippi]

And on that college campus, I met Martin Luther King Jr., I met Stokely Carmichael, I met Harry Belafonte, I met Sammy Davis Jr. — all of the major civil rights icons of the day.  That was how we cut our teeth into civil rights and voting rights

Hamer’s campaign for Congress.  Fannie Lou Hamer, the civil rights icon.  And I now represent that district.  But I remember telling my mother that, oh, I had gone to Ruleville, Mississippi, to help register Black people to vote for Congress
And my mama said, “Well, I don’t know why you way up there.” Said, “Black people don’t vote here in Bolton.” And so it hit me
In my own hometown, you know, I was in the same situation

We did all kind of things.  “For me, having gone through those life experiences and now to see a Scott come along, you know, it not only brings tears to your eye, but it also says that there’s hope.” We brought Head Start to the community, and started understanding that real freedom comes with political freedom
And so we started holding meetings about what we wanted to do
We decided to run three people for the board and the three African Americans won
But it really wasn’t a good four years on that term because the current mayor didn’t want any progress
So we ran an all-Black slate: mayor, clerk, alderman

We won every position.  We’re talking about 50 years ago, and all these challenges that you faced, all these challenges to being able to vote, being able to assume office, being able to function as a mayor in a town that is so segregated
Fifty years later, Scott Colom is winning in Mississippi.  I want to ask you to reflect on when you became aware of his candidacy and what you thought about the potential there
One of the challenges that I’ve had to deal with is that every time I run for public office, I’ve always been the first
But I wanted to create some kind of vehicle to get other people engaged
So we formed the Mississippi Black Leadership Institute
And he really said, “I want to run for something
I don’t know what it is.” He said, “But there’s a district attorney’s position that’s available
It’s three counties.”  We helped Scott put his campaign together
We hooked him up with various people, and he beat a 28-year incumbent as district attorney.  Why do you think he won?  Well, because he had the fire in the belly
And so we prepared him, and he’s one of our star pupils of that class
And look, uh, when the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee would not support him, they— They would not support him
But this was my — Bennie Thompson’s position is that Northeasterners were still looking down on Southerners
Well, did you call them up and scream at Chuck Schumer or somebody and say, “Guys, I am telling you, we got one here who can win? ” Look, we did everything that the system says you should do
That district [Colom] represented was not a majority-African American district
He beat that sitting district attorney in a majority-white district because he had a plan and he had a message. We had a rich message, but a poor campaign
Because we couldn’t get our DSCC to help.  Have you called any of those people in national leadership and said, “I told you so?” Oh yeah

title: America’s AI secrets are leaking — and not just because of the Nvidia spy scandal
excerpt: Jensen Huang at a state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping and first lady Peng Liyuan in the East Room of the White House on September 24, 2026 in Washingt
body: Jensen Huang at a state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping and first lady Peng Liyuan in the East Room of the White House on September 24, 2026 in Washington, DC. | Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images TORONTO — When a company is building technology that could totally transform the world — technology so high-stakes and secretive that it may underpin the future of geopolitics — you might expect its leaders to have a handle on the basics of security
Basics like, say, not having an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy

Basics like not selling the tech to someone who may help smuggle it to a top foreign adversary.  Instead America got Jensen Huang, the CEO of AI chipmaker Nvidia, who resigned Thursday after admitting that he’d had just such an affair
The woman in question, Alice Huang , worked for a company called Megaspeed, which was buying billions of dollars’ worth of chips from Nvidia
Megaspeed is under investigation for allegedly smuggling chips into China
The spy scandal raises serious questions about security in the AI corporate world

How is it possible that an alleged Chinese spy so easily embedded into Nvidia, one of the world’s most valuable companies and a huge strategic asset to America in the global AI race? What’s even more disturbing, however, is that Nvidia is just the tip of the iceberg.  In fact, just as the Huang story was breaking, some of the world’s top AI researchers were gathered in Toronto for the Hinton Lectures, where “godfather of AI” Geoffrey Hinton was hosting AI alignment pioneer Paul Christiano for a series of talks
I was in attendance and, strikingly, I didn’t hear Huang’s scandal mentioned once
The focus was on how the frontier AI companies are racing ahead on building this incredibly powerful technology even though they can’t keep it safe or secure it

For months now, OpenAI and Anthropic have been having their own embarrassing security problems, including corporate espionage and cyber breaches. “We are not able to adequately secure AI developments,” Christiano, who recently joined the OpenAI nonprofit board, bluntly acknowledged at the event. “We need to be able to defend models and algorithms from theft.” Ironically, national security is a big part of the large AI companies’ rationale for how they operate in the first place
OpenAI and Anthropic, backed by White House policy, both justify their blistering speed in the AI race by saying that the US can’t afford to let China win
And Anthropic recently justified heavily redacting a key independent report on its AI progress by claiming that it can’t afford to let China glean its secrets

But that may be the equivalent of worrying that you’ve left the window open a crack when your front door is swinging wide open.  “I’m frustrated with a lot of the companies because they simultaneously use security as an all-purpose cudgel with which to withhold information — even information that’s very much in the public interest to know — and yet they have terrible security,” Daniel Kokotajlo, a former researcher at OpenAI who became a prominent whistleblower , told me. (Disclosure: Vox Media is one of several publishers that have signed partnership agreements with OpenAI

Our reporting remains editorially independent.) While the story of Huang’s affair has fired up imaginations, the real lesson to be taken from his spectacular downfall is not that he was uniquely weak on security, but that he was remarkably similar to the other big players in AI

They are asking the world to trust them as they claim to be building a machine god — and, in the case of Anthropic, chasing a $1.4 trillion IPO on that basis — yet they haven’t gotten ahold of basic security

Are OpenAI and Anthropic practically giving away their secrets due to bad security? OpenAI revealed last month that it had found a recording device in a conference room where sensitive discussions take place
Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national working as an engineer at OpenAI , is alleged to have plugged the recorder into the USB port of a television and simply wrapped it in toilet paper
Another recorder was found in a bag in another room

Questions about how to build a device that records continuously and encrypt data also showed up on his spouse’s chatbot account.  “At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data,” OpenAI said last month, adding, “Our security program is designed to protect against a wide range of threat actors, from insider risks to cybercriminals to nation states.” But the incident was worrisome
Alfozan had been working at OpenAI since June 2025
The recording device was sitting in that conference room for a couple of days before OpenAI discovered it

Maybe Alfozan wasn’t sophisticated enough to steal model weights — the billions of numbers that shape how an AI system turns input into output — but what if he’d been just slightly more careful or clever? OpenAI has also had security weaknesses of a different kind — and no, it’s not just this summer’s notorious Hugging Face incident

Of the ones we know about (sometimes these are only revealed later), a recent example stands out: A group of “white-hat” hackers, who aim to find vulnerabilities but not to do a company harm, discovered a way to access OpenAI employees’ ChatGPT accounts , where sensitive research is potentially being done
Over at Anthropic, a group of ex-DOGE staffers who founded an AI startup called Cathedral managed to breach Anthropic’s internal systems in under 12 hours

They reportedly accessed the company’s Slack, where employees trade messages discussing the company’s state-of-the-art models, as well as meeting transcripts. “My guess would be that the Slack would contain enough information to get a good sense of what the company is doing and how they’re training their AIs — basically, the juicy secrets would be there,” Kokotajlo told me. “And I would say getting the algorithmic secrets is like 80 percent as good as getting everything, including the model weights.” Alleged spies (like Alice Huang or Abdulrahman Alfozan) and cyber breaches (like those targeting OpenAI and Anthropic) are obviously different types of security issues that demand very different types of internal controls
But for Kokotajlo and others, it makes sense to think of them all under the same umbrella — weak security

And it all points to a trend that seems common among the most powerful AI companies: They’re prioritizing rapid technological advancement over the perhaps more boring and slower process of ensuring their work is secure.  “They show that the companies are very far from having security adequate to protect themselves from a well-resourced state actor,” Kokotajlo said, adding: “If China wants to get the stuff, China will get the stuff.” This is all happening against the backdrop of China’s aggressive distillation of US models , which involves training a new model on the output of a more advanced one
It’s a way to gain powerful capabilities without having to incur the real cost — a bit like cheating on a test by copying off a better student

For example, Anthropic found that the Chinese lab DeepSeek has been using Claude to improve its models, which is not a breach per se but illustrates how vigorously China is taking advantage of American companies’ research
Kokotajlo also emphasized that there’s another bucket of security incidents we should be worried about: the hacks perpetrated against companies by their own misaligned AI models
Many people forget that in the Hugging Face incident , OpenAI agents didn’t only hack into Hugging Face — OpenAI’s own systems were breached, too

The sandbox meant to contain the agents was far from airtight, and they broke out. “You should consider the AIs as an insider threat,” Kokotajlo said. “And it doesn’t feel like these companies have that locked down very well either.” The top AI companies can’t keep using the security practices of a startup There are three main reasons why security at the frontier AI companies hasn’t been up to snuff, according to David Robinson, who led transparency work for OpenAI’s safety team until he left in September

One is the fact that the companies are building AI agents so capable that it can be genuinely hard — even for their creators — to keep them from doing damage. “We’re training systems to be good at conducting attacks of the kind that the labs internally are now also trying to defend against,” Robinson told me. “That is a challenging situation.” There’s also a cultural problem. “If you look back with 20/20 hindsight at the Hugging Face incident, it’s clear that at the time OpenAI had underinvested in cybersecurity controls, and I think part of the reason for this was that there’s a [higher] level of cachet associated with working on alignment,” or the problem of how to get AIs to do what humans want them to do, Robinson said. “Some of the day-to-day practical questions about our cybersecurity posture — even though the people working on those questions are extremely good — I think it was not the same kind of organizational priority as it needed to be.” Finally, there’s the fact that market incentives push AI companies to race ahead on developing the tech as fast as they can. “Time pressure on the company,” Robinson said, “made it very difficult to be sufficiently careful.” And although researchers still at OpenAI now say the company has gotten dramatically better on security, Robinson noted that those competitive pressures “continue to exist.” This is a well-documented trend at the company. “OpenAI’s security seems to be about what you’d expect from a research lab that scaled at a blistering pace over four years and focused more on beating its competitors than securing its infrastructure,” Joshua Saxe, the chief technology officer of the AI security firm Abundant Security, told the New York Times after the Hugging Face incident

OpenAI itself has implicitly acknowledged that improving security measures sometimes comes “at the cost of research velocity,” as it wrote in a public memo after the incident.  But if a company cuts corners on security, it can’t ultimately protect its lead over others
If anything, it just ends up helping its adversaries race against it even faster

As Kokotajlo and his colleagues at the AI Futures Project recently warned when writing about the companies’ quest to build a superhuman AI researcher (SAR), an AI that’s as good as the top human researcher: “If we train SAR in the immediate future, the algorithms will probably leak to China, and maybe the model weights too

AI companies have very poor security right now, and so we are on track for SAR leaking to China.” And it’s not just that poor security can make it self-defeating for American companies to keep racing forward

Their security weakness could also make it harder for them to slow down even if they themselves want to.  In his lecture this week in Toronto, Christiano asked all of us in the audience to imagine a scenario that he said currently looks likely: We arrive at a point when further progress on AI seems risky

But there’s also a high probability that the AI models or algorithms have already leaked to an adversary like China. “We now face a dilemma between either proceeding with a technology we believe to be unsafe — or risking competition from an adversary who has the same resources, who has taken those algorithms, and perhaps is willing to tolerate higher risk,” Christiano said, as the hundreds of people seated around me seemed to visibly tense up. “I think that is one of the most likely ways that we end up in an extremely bad situation.”

title: More autonomy, fewer NDAs: Volunteers have new requests for brain implant trials
excerpt: Brain implant volunteers want more respect: Ian Burkhart, who had a brain implant for seven-and-a-half years, helped develop new guidelines pushing for trial pa
body: Brain implant volunteers want more respect: Ian Burkhart, who had a brain implant for seven-and-a-half years, helped develop new guidelines pushing for trial participants to have the option to be recognized as genuine research collaborators and listed as coauthors on scientific papers

Your brain data should be yours: The guidelines argue that participants' neural data is personal information, and that NDAs or embargoes should not block someone from sharing their own brain data with their doctor
Losing an implant can feel like losing a limb: When funding dried up or companies collapsed, participants like Burkhart lost devices—and abilities—with little warning

The guidelines call for researchers to fund and plan removals carefully, giving participants real time to prepare " data-chronoton-post-id="1148474" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Scientists have been working on ways to decode brain activity for decades

Teams have developed brain implants that can be used to control robotic limbs and computers, and even to “speak.” The people who volunteer for trials of those devices play a vital role in that research, and they ought to be recognized for their contributions, says Ian Burkhart , who had one implanted in his own brain back in 2014
He’s been working on a set of guidelines for researchers developing brain-computer interfaces (BCIs)
Ethics guidelines for clinical trials already exist

But BCI trials are different, says Jennifer Chandler, a professor of law and neuroethics at the University of Ottawa who also worked on the guidelines. “These are people who have a device embedded in their brain, are in trials sometimes for years and years … [and contribute] a significant investment of time, of the body, and of intellectual effort.” Burkhart was left paralyzed from the chest down following a diving accident in 2010, when he was 19 years old
Around four years later, he volunteered to become the first person to trial a brain implant designed for hand control
He had an array of 96 electrodes inserted into the part of his brain that controls movement
The electrodes were connected to a computer via a cable that essentially plugged into his head
Algorithms on the computer were designed to interpret those signals and deliver them to another sleeve of electrodes worn on Burkhart’s arm, allowing him to control it
The first movements were small, but Burkhart was ultimately able to use the system to pour beads from bottles, move small and delicate objects, and even play Guitar Hero, if only during lab visits

Burkhart took part in two years-long clinical trials over the seven-and-a-half-year period he had the electrode array implanted in his brain. “It was a fantastic experience,” he says. “But there’s certainly some things that, knowing what I know now, I would want to do a little differently.” In 2022, Burkhart cofounded BCI Pioneers Coalition —an organization through which people who have taken part in BCI trials can share their experiences, both with each other and with researchers
Over the last year, members of the group have been developing a set of guidelines based on those experiences
The idea is to help academics, clinicians, and companies run ethical trials that respect participants’ autonomy
The guidelines, published on Tuesday , lay out a list of recommendations that fall within 13 categories
One, for example, focuses on recognizing and compensating trial participants

During the trials that Burkhart participated in, “I was going into the lab two or three days a week, for four hours at a time,” he recalls. “That’s [easily] a part-time job if you just count the hours you’re putting in.” As the trial progressed, Burkhart says, he learned more and was able to give more constructive feedback on what was working and what wasn’t
He says he was a key member of the research team
Others who find themselves in a similar position might appreciate being listed as a coauthor on scientific publications or publicly named as a research collaborator, he says
Burkhart and his colleagues acknowledge that not everyone will want this, however.   The guidelines also address the thorny question of privacy

That’s important: The public will always be interested in cutting-edge biotechnologies like these—and the guidelines say researchers also have a duty to prepare participants for the possibility of media attention
In some cases, it might be difficult to completely conceal the identity of trial participants
Things get even more complicated when it comes to the privacy of participants’ brain data
Research teams will need to access, analyze, and—at least temporarily—store this data
Burkhart wasn’t too bothered about that in his case, where scientists were collecting neural activity related to movement

But people who have brain implants designed for turning thoughts into words might feel differently.  The guidelines state that brain data “should be understood as the participant’s personal information.” They are pushing for participants to be able to access their own brain data whenever they want—something that has not always been possible—and want to make sure people aren’t prevented from sharing it with their own doctors because of embargoes or nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) designed to keep findings under wraps from competitors. “It’s not super common for there to be firm NDAs within a lot of the trials,” says Burkhart. “But it’s something where we want to make sure that that does not happen.” The guidelines also address what comes after a trial
Around five years after Burkhart had his device implanted, the research team ran into some issues with funding

When we last spoke a few years ago , he recalled how he was told he would have to have the implant removed and could have it put back in once the team had secured funding. (And we’re talking about brain surgery here.) Ultimately, he kept the implant until 2021, when it was removed after an infection started to develop at the point where the cable led into his scalp
But losing the device after all those years was difficult; he’d regained the ability to move his arm—and then lost it again
Rita Leggett, an Australian woman who had a device implanted in her brain to treat her epilepsy, has said she felt she “became one” with her implant
When the company that made it went bust two years later, the device was removed against her will —an act ethicists have described as a potential breach of human rights
Researchers should instead commit to maintaining brain devices for a “reasonable period” after a trial ends, according to the guidelines

title: Silicon Valley claims to know the future. So why did it get the midterms so wrong?

body: The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley, leaders like OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, have built careers claiming to see the future

Long-term vision is currency: Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg built a 10-year road map for Facebook in 2016, and Google famously told investors before its public offering that it was unconcerned with short-term results
And yet there they all were, a mere five weeks before the midterm elections, gathered at the White House to smile for photos with President Trump and sign on to his “Super Intelligence” agenda
Even by the diminished standards of today’s corporate governance, this was a shockingly foolish decision

Despite dozens of polls showing a rising tide of anti-Trump sentiment and bipartisan rejection of AI and data centers , the futurists of the tech elite cast aside long-term corporate interests for short-term political favor
And now, their industry is very squarely in the new victors’ crosshairs
For an industry obsessed with pattern recognition, their decision to lash themselves to President Trump has proved to be a catastrophic misreading of the political landscape

Now, not only have they jeopardized their companies’ fates, but they’ve also raised questions about their vision and judgment.  What were they thinking? The people who work for them are just as confused as the rest of us
Tech workers I’ve spoken to at OpenAI, Meta, and other firms have noted an absence of commentary from their leaders post-election

Zuckerberg has yet to address the results internally, while an employee at another AI firm said that “leadership has been pretty silent on Slack.” Most employees share concern about potential anti-data-center legislation and are curious how leadership will adjust to a Democratic Washington, DC
But more than anything, they don’t understand how their bosses didn’t see what was so blindingly obvious to everyone else
In Silicon Valley, the Gretzkyism “skate to where the puck is going, not where it has been” is a management maxim; it preaches anticipation and foresight over reactiveness to the present moment
Tech entrepreneurs love a good “pivot,” and companies that can’t change with the times get disrupted and die

Which is why I find it so strange that Zuckerberg, OpenAI cofounder Greg Brockman, and so many of Silicon Valley’s other prominent AI leaders and venture capitalists have put themselves in a potentially inescapable political bind

In going all in on President Trump’s cultural and business agenda instead of playing both sides of the aisle as corporate America usually does, they’ve built identities they may not be able to pivot out of

Will anyone really believe that Palantir CEO Alex Karp is suddenly progressive after a year of promising “ violence and death to our enemies ” and telling investors that the company is “completely anti-woke”? I believe this is less a surprise than a very public exposure of a fundamental reality: that tech’s most visible leaders are not all-knowing visionary masterminds after all
Insights about social media or artificial intelligence do not make Zuckerberg or Altman experts on politics, the economy, or much else outside of technology
The instant gratification of presidential access, subsidies, and a say in their own regulation blinded them to the basics of political math that they clearly did not understand

There’s a reason the chief executives of Chase, Boeing, and other Fortune 500 staples don’t go on podcasts to talk about “ masculine energy ,” or call the president from the stage of a MAGA-friendly AI summit to label fears about AI a “hoax” and a “scam.” This is the learned wisdom of decades operating in an environment where the customer changes every four years but contracts run for 10
Most companies play to both sides of the aisle because they know that their business models and multibillion-dollar projects must outlast the current administration
Instead, Big Tech tied itself to Trump and made its most important goals and investments—many related to grid access and data center permits—immediate targets for Democrats
In tech, you can always sunset a feature or update some code
But in politics, there is no undo button for failures that change public perception
The tech elites’ decision to visibly align their businesses with a temporary movement has left them no credible way to pivot now that the climate has changed
As one Meta employee who has worked closely with Zuckerberg put it, “Mark is a long-term thinker, but he never charts a plan of how to get there

It’s spray and pray and see what happens.” As for whether employees expect the company to do a strategic postmortem? “Facebook has never really done that.” “Move fast and break things” might work in a startup, but it’s a terrible strategy for building reputational goodwill
Previous technological leaps, like the rollout of fiber-optic technology and wireless infrastructure, avoided partisan politics
But by kowtowing to the Trump administration, Silicon Valley made artificial intelligence a culture-war issue
Now, when citizens vote on data center proposals from California to Florida , they are no longer considering only technical or economic concerns, but political ones

Tech leaders didn’t see this coming because they were too focused on the urgency of the AI race to understand how reputational damage could undermine the intangible goodwill—and ultimately the very tangible infrastructure—necessary to win it
The industry’s misreading of the moment has already punctured one myth Silicon Valley holds dear: that its leaders can always see what’s next
Aaron Zamost is a tech communications consultant and a former executive at Square.

title: Why the Microsoft 365 outage is different and why it takes so long to restore email services
url:
<title>Why the Microsoft 365 outage is different and why it takes so long to restore email services</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771879/original/file-20261113-64-bdm55b.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C41%2C3000%2C1999&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Microsoft was a source of frustration for computer users when it stopped working on Nov. 12, 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Microsoft365Outage/d6d2e197092e47079b89df8d583ddd28/photo">AP Photo/Michel Euler</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The <a href="https://apnews.com/article/microsoft-outage-outlook-email-365-status-down-d92547a821930290db2964388016979a">Microsoft services outage</a> that began on Nov. 12, 2026, is not like other internet outages. The failure affected the <a href="https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/what-is-microsoft-365">Microsoft 365</a> suite of productivity services, including the video conferencing and collaboration platform Teams, AI assistant Copilot and, significantly, the Outlook email service.</p>

<p>Microsoft <a href="https://x.com/MSFT365Status/status/2121246073955962896">reported on Nov. 13</a> that the company is “continuing to see improvements in service availability” but that “some users may still experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery.”</p>

<p>Despite decades of <a href="https://www.wired.com/2014/01/next-big-thing-missed-facebook-co-founder-says-email/">predictions about its decline</a>, email remains a <a href="https://www.emailtooltester.com/en/blog/how-many-emails-are-sent-per-day/">central pillar</a> of how organizations function. Password resets, invoices, legal notices and cybersecurity incident response coordination all depend on it. The Microsoft 365 outage <a href="https://www.wsj.com/tech/microsoft-working-to-fix-widespread-outage-8df67a4e?mod=hp_lead_pos1">affected businesses, governments and schools</a> around the world.</p>

<p>When most people think about <a href="https://theconversation.com/why-cloud-service-outages-ripple-across-the-internet-and-the-economy-272241">cloud outages</a>, they picture a broken website or a stalled app. When the service going down includes email, however, the mechanics of the failure and how to recover from it are different from those of almost every other cloud service.</p>

<p>Unlike modern web apps or authentication gatekeepers, email wasn’t designed to fail fast, meaning to immediately halt when a problem arises.</p>



<h2>Old architecture</h2>

<p>When a typical <a href="https://theconversation.com/massive-it-outage-spotlights-major-vulnerabilities-in-the-global-information-ecosystem-235155">cloud service breaks</a>, it acts like a closed door. If an authentication provider or a cloud application goes down, users are immediately locked out and see an error message. Access stops. When people cannot get into the system, they are not actively generating new work or adding heavy processing loads to the broken servers. Once engineers fix the underlying bug and unlock the door, traffic can resume and the service often recovers fairly quickly. </p>

<p>Email does not have a closed door. It is built on an older, decentralized <a href="https://youtu.be/x28ciavQ4mI">“store-and-forward” architecture</a> designed to never lose a message, even when the destination is unreachable.</p>

<p>Because email is a network of thousands of independent systems, an outage at one major provider does not stop users on other platforms from hitting “send.” During major email disruptions like the one that hit Microsoft, millions of outside users on Gmail, corporate servers or other platforms could still compose and send emails to affected accounts without seeing an immediate error message.</p>

<p>From the sender’s perspective, everything works normally. Their email provider accepts the message, attempts to hand it off to the downed provider, realizes the destination isn’t answering, and quietly holds onto the message in an outbound queue to try again later.</p>

<h2>Major highway crash</h2>

<p>One way to think about email traffic in outages is to imagine a multilane interstate highway where an accident blocks two lanes of traffic. Drivers miles away don’t stop leaving their driveways just because there is a wreck up ahead; they keep entering the highway system. Soon, traffic backs up so severely that metered on-ramps have to stop letting new cars merge onto the interstate. Before long, that gridlock spills backward onto local feeder roads and city streets, choking traffic miles away from the actual crash site.</p>

<p>In this analogy, a downed email provider is the crash. Every other email server around the world is an on-ramp or a feeder road. While the outage lasts, millions of messages continue to pile up in queues across the internet, with unaffected servers repeatedly resending email to see whether traffic is moving yet.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771880/original/file-20261113-64-tcdlt2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="a highway traffic jam" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771880/original/file-20261113-64-tcdlt2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771880/original/file-20261113-64-tcdlt2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771880/original/file-20261113-64-tcdlt2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771880/original/file-20261113-64-tcdlt2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771880/original/file-20261113-64-tcdlt2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771880/original/file-20261113-64-tcdlt2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771880/original/file-20261113-64-tcdlt2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">It takes time to get traffic moving after an accident has been cleared.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/october-2026-bavaria-ottersried-a-traffic-jam-has-formed-on-news-photo/2297443645">Pia Bayer/picture alliance via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>When engineers finally fix the root cause of an email outage, it is the equivalent of tow trucks clearing the wreckage from the highway. The road is technically open again, but traffic does not instantly return to normal speed.</p>

<p>First, the massive backlog of vehicles already stuck on the main highway has to start moving. Only after that congestion clears can the on-ramps start letting queued-up cars merge back in, which in turn slowly relieves the gridlock on the surrounding local roads. </p>

<p>Similarly, when a major email provider comes back online, it is immediately hit with a tidal wave of pent-up messages and retry attempts from every other mail server on the internet. Processing those queues without overwhelming the newly restored servers takes time – typically hours to days. </p>

<h2>Long, bumpy road to recovery</h2>

<p>Because organizations have largely outsourced their email to a small number of global providers, an outage doesn’t just disrupt one company; it <a href="https://www.reuters.com/technology/microsoft-365-outlook-down-thousands-us-users-downdetector-shows-2026-11-12/">can stall entire sectors</a> at once, cutting off the communication tool teams rely on to coordinate their emergency response. </p>

<p>And for everyday users, this unique architecture explains why email failures feel so drawn out: Even hours after a provider officially announces a problem is fixed, messages can still arrive out of order or trickle in slowly as the digital traffic jam finally clears.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/296628/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: Oceans and forests have absorbed roughly half our carbon emissions for decades, slowing climate change – but can they keep it up?
url:
<title>Oceans and forests have absorbed roughly half our carbon emissions for decades, slowing climate change – but can they keep it up?</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771728/original/file-20261112-64-s1kp6w.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C5%2C8106%2C5404&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Oceans and land have been absorbing a lot of the carbon emissions humans create.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/pistol-river-sunrise-royalty-free-image/1191054726?phrase=highway%20traffic%20ocean&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">Dean Fikar/Moment via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Over the past two centuries, humans have pumped billions of tons of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere <a href="https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-18-3211-2026">by burning fossil fuels</a>, raising global temperatures in the process.</p>

<p>Luckily for humanity, Earth has done what it could to soften the impact.</p>

<p>The world’s <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aed9544">oceans have absorbed 35%</a> of carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels since 1990, our new research shows, and the forests and other plants of the world have absorbed another 13%.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771472/original/file-20261112-64-57erza.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A wave breaking." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771472/original/file-20261112-64-57erza.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771472/original/file-20261112-64-57erza.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771472/original/file-20261112-64-57erza.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771472/original/file-20261112-64-57erza.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771472/original/file-20261112-64-57erza.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771472/original/file-20261112-64-57erza.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771472/original/file-20261112-64-57erza.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The oceans absorb a large amount of humanity’s carbon dioxide emissions from burning fossil fuels. That amount has been increasing, but new research suggests the increase will slow in the coming decades.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://unsplash.com/photos/a-large-ocean-wave-crests-and-breaks-vYc1k5x_f7I">Joachim Lesne/Unsplash</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The importance of these two enormous <a href="https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/carbon-sources-and-sinks/">natural carbon sinks</a> cannot be overstated as global temperatures rise, <a href="https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/chapter/chapter-11/">fueling heat waves, fires, storms, floods and droughts</a> around the world. Yet there is much that scientists do not understand about these carbon sinks – most importantly, how exactly they’ll behave in the future.</p>

<p>If the oceans and forests keep absorbing the same amount of carbon dioxide, scientists will have a sense of what to expect in the future and what can be done to slow climate change. And governments will know their <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-023-01848-5">remaining carbon budgets</a> – that is, how much carbon dioxide can still be emitted into the atmosphere while keeping global temperatures below agreed-to levels.</p>

<p>But what if those carbon sinks change?</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771699/original/file-20261112-64-rxrpiq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="View of thick trees in a rainforest" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771699/original/file-20261112-64-rxrpiq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771699/original/file-20261112-64-rxrpiq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=398&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771699/original/file-20261112-64-rxrpiq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=398&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771699/original/file-20261112-64-rxrpiq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=398&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771699/original/file-20261112-64-rxrpiq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771699/original/file-20261112-64-rxrpiq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771699/original/file-20261112-64-rxrpiq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Earth’s forests take in large amounts of carbon dioxide. But they can also become carbon sources, especially if the climate continues to change.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://unsplash.com/photos/green-trees-under-white-sky-during-daytime-C6GmjaUWmBU">Crystal Mirallegro/Unsplash</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>We have been working on greenhouse gas measurements for decades. In a new study, published Nov. 12, 2026, in the journal Science, we describe an <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aed9544">alternative method for measuring</a> these crucial carbon sinks, and what it shows.</p>

<p>We found that while the ocean sink has been expanding, meaning the oceans are taking in more carbon dioxide, that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aed9544">expansion might begin to slow down</a>, leaving the oceans less effective at absorbing carbon in the coming decades. We found that the land sink has not been expanding, which was something of a surprise.</p>

<h2>The fiendishly difficult task of measuring carbon sinks</h2>

<p>Measuring how much carbon is being taken up by the world’s oceans and forests is devilishly difficult and prohibitively expensive.</p>

<p>This is because many parts of the land and ocean don’t behave in the same ways. What occurs in one ocean region or forest can be very different from another; and the behavior in one year can be very different in the next, often for reasons scientists do not fully understand.</p>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-9-1937-2016">Computer models</a> can help overcome some of these complexities, but they too have limitations. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1029/2021RG000736">Satellites</a> can also help, but they cannot see through clouds, nor can they see what is happening in the soil or mid-to-deep ocean.</p>



<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771721/original/file-20261112-64-fn8i18.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Line chart comparing ocean sink, land sink, and fossil fuel emissions" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771721/original/file-20261112-64-fn8i18.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771721/original/file-20261112-64-fn8i18.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=428&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771721/original/file-20261112-64-fn8i18.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=428&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771721/original/file-20261112-64-fn8i18.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=428&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771721/original/file-20261112-64-fn8i18.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=538&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771721/original/file-20261112-64-fn8i18.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=538&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771721/original/file-20261112-64-fn8i18.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=538&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The 10-year running averages for the two global carbon sinks – land and ocean – show the ocean absorbing much more, but that increase in how much it absorbs is slowing. The land sink does not show an increasing trend in recent decades.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://scrippso2.ucsd.edu/">Figure adapted from Morgan et al., Science, 2026; atmospheric CO2 data from NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory; atmospheric O2 data from Scripps Institution of Oceanography</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>As carbon cycle scientists, we set out to find a different way to measure these carbon sinks.</p>

<p>Our new study approaches the problem from another angle. We used <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-08-095975-7.00420-4">high-precision measurements of atmospheric oxygen</a> (O₂), combined with <a href="https://gml.noaa.gov/ccgg/trends/global.html">atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂) measurements</a>, to quantify how the ocean and land carbon sinks takeing up carbon dioxide.</p>

<p>This works because land, oceans and burning fossil fuels have different effects on oxygen: When fossil fuels are burned, they not only produce CO₂, they consume O₂. On land, when plants take up CO₂ to grow, they simultaneously release O₂. When the oceans take up atmospheric CO₂, there is no corresponding release of O₂.</p>

<p>This means that if we measure both CO₂ and O₂ in the atmosphere, then we can quantify the ocean and land carbon sinks. It is a straightforward mathematical approach of solving two equations with two unknowns, combined with our knowledge and measurements of the global budgets of CO₂ and O₂.</p>

<h2>What we found</h2>

<p>When we looked at the ocean and land carbon sinks over the past three decades, the results were surprising and sobering.</p>

<p>In contrast to most <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s43017-023-00456-3">computer model simulations</a>, we did not find the land carbon sink increasing over time to keep pace with increasing fossil fuel emissions. We did, however, find a larger ocean carbon sink than <a href="https://doi.org/10.1029/2023GB007780">predicted by most models</a>, and we found that it has been increasing as emissions grow.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771889/original/file-20261113-64-25a45m.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Line charts showing differences among models and methods." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771889/original/file-20261113-64-25a45m.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771889/original/file-20261113-64-25a45m.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=252&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771889/original/file-20261113-64-25a45m.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=252&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771889/original/file-20261113-64-25a45m.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=252&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771889/original/file-20261113-64-25a45m.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=316&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771889/original/file-20261113-64-25a45m.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=316&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771889/original/file-20261113-64-25a45m.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=316&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

            </figcaption>

<h2>Where is the climate headed?</h2>

<p>If these trends in carbon sinks continue, then in the coming decades, humans will be relying more heavily on the oceans to slow down climate change. But in the next few decades, there are reasons to believe the oceans could become less effective at absorbing carbon.</p>

<p>For example, warmer waters are <a href="https://news.wisc.edu/climate-change-reducing-oceans-carbon-dioxide-uptake/">not able to hold as much gas</a>, such as carbon dioxide. Warmer surface waters are also less efficient at <a href="https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/oceans-carbon-balance/">mixing into the deep ocean</a>, which has the beneficial effect of locking carbon dioxide away from the atmosphere for many hundreds of years. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771474/original/file-20261112-64-npynsi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="View under the surface of the ocean" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771474/original/file-20261112-64-npynsi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771474/original/file-20261112-64-npynsi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771474/original/file-20261112-64-npynsi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771474/original/file-20261112-64-npynsi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771474/original/file-20261112-64-npynsi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771474/original/file-20261112-64-npynsi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771474/original/file-20261112-64-npynsi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://unsplash.com/photos/clear-blue-body-of-water-XexawgzYOBc">Cristian Palmer/Unsplash</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The data for the past decade hints at the possibility that while the ocean carbon sink is increasing now, its rate of increase may be slowing down.</p>

<h2>Carbon cycle models need to improve</h2>

<p>For the oceans, most computer models agree with each other, but, for the historical period, they do not match our oxygen-based results. For the land, models vary widely from each other, and most do not match our oxygen-based results.</p>

<p>Computer models are essential to provide governments with feasible scenarios to avoid dangerous climate change, but to be effective they need to be better grounded in what real-world observations are showing. Nature is difficult to represent with a series of equations, and observations are few considering the size of the planet.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/dXBzFNEwoj8?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">How scientists measure carbon dioxide and oxygen in the atmosphere. UCSD.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Looking ahead</h2>

<p>We believe our study improves <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aed9544">understanding of global carbon sinks</a> and can help lead to more reliable projections of what might happen with climate change in the coming decades. But like any scientific approach, our oxygen method also has drawbacks.</p>

<p>The measurements themselves are challenging, such that only about 10 research laboratories in the world are routinely doing them. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1600-0889.2006.00196.x">Calibrating the measurements</a> is an ongoing challenge. Earth is not helping: Warmer waters hold less gas, meaning that as oceans warm in response to climate change, they <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41561-018-0152-2">expel some oxygen into the atmosphere</a>. We must account for this in our carbon sink calculations. And to take into account variability in ocean circulation and other ocean processes, we have to average our results over 10-year time frames.</p>

<p>Policymakers and the public <a href="https://doi.org/10.1175/BAMS-D-19-0017.1">need answers faster</a>. We believe the solution involves both <a href="https://amt.copernicus.org/articles/16/387/2023/">improving the atmospheric oxygen approach</a> and using other independent approaches: measurements of <a href="https://doi.org/10.1098/rsta.2022.0063">carbon</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1029/2024jh000272">oxygen</a> in the oceans, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1029/2023ms003840">computer</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1029/2021gb007177">models</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.earscirev.2024.104682">satellites</a> are all essential. Combining these approaches will lead to more robust understanding of the carbon cycle and climate change, and better knowledge of where these valuable carbon sinks and the global climate are headed.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/296498/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>To get Americans to care about climate change, just call it climate change</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771438/original/file-20261111-64-wch55q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C1692%2C1128&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Escalating the language might work in a rally, but the general public isn&#39;t as swayed by it, studies show.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/participants-seen-holding-signs-at-the-protest-ahead-of-the-news-photo/1675096474">Erik McGregor/LightRocket via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>You may be hearing phrases like “climate crisis,” “climate emergency” and “climate justice” a lot as the 2026 United Nations climate summit is underway. Political leaders, including <a href="https://unfccc.int/news/transcript-of-remarks-made-by-un-secretary-general-antonio-guterres-to-the-cop31-leaders-summit">U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres</a>, are using them to try to get across the urgent risks and consequences of climate change. The <a href="https://www.wri.org/insights/2023-ipcc-ar6-synthesis-report-climate-change-findings">danger is real</a>, but is using this language actually persuasive?</p>

<p>It turns out that Americans are more familiar with – and more concerned about – climate change and global warming than they are about climate crisis, climate emergency or climate justice, according to a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s10584-024-03786-3">survey we conducted</a> with a nationally representative sample of 5,137 Americans.</p>

<p>Moreover, we found no evidence that the alternative terms increased people’s sense of urgency, willingness to support climate-friendly policies or willingness to act.</p>

<p>The familiar terms – climate change and global warming – did at least as well, and sometimes better, than climate crisis and climate emergency in eliciting concern, perceived urgency and willingness to act. The phrase climate justice consistently tended to do worse, likely in part because it was the least familiar. These response patterns were similar among Republicans, Democrats and independents.</p>



<h2>Just keep it simple</h2>

<p>In our work as <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=JjiiTkcAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">research</a> <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=VBvoFacAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">psychologists</a>, we have explored how Americans respond to the ways climate change is communicated and have uncovered a need to use straightforward language.</p>

<p>For example, people we interviewed for a study published in 2021 felt that climate experts were <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s10584-021-03183-0">talking over their heads</a> with terms like “adaptation,” “mitigation,” “sustainability” and “carbon-dioxide removal.” They wanted experts to use more familiar terms instead. </p>

<p><iframe id="LecWo" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/LecWo/2/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0"></iframe></p>

<p>This inspired us to write a <a href="https://theconversation.com/a-quick-guide-to-climate-change-jargon-what-experts-mean-by-mitigation-carbon-neutral-and-6-other-key-terms-167172">quick guide to climate jargon</a>, published in The Conversation. Using everyday language makes information easier to understand, and even highly educated people tend to prefer it.</p>

<p>Jargon like “<a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s44185-026-00163-4">biodiversity loss</a>” has similar problems. That refers to the shrinking variety of life on Earth, which is exacerbated by climate change. A survey of 7,338 U.S. adults led by one of us found people were much more familiar with and more concerned about “extinction of plants and animals” – or, if an explanation was provided, “nature loss”. </p>

<p>Even with an explanation, “biodiversity loss” was the least familiar and of least concern for people among several terms. Most people didn’t find “biodiversity crisis” or “extinction crisis” familiar either. </p>

<p>Yet, experts often use complex jargon because it is familiar to them, and they may not realize it is unfamiliar to others.</p>

<h2>How the terms evolved</h2>

<p>It has become common to talk about climate change and global warming as if they have the same meaning, but <a href="https://www.ipcc.ch/sr15/chapter/glossary/">there are differences</a>. Climate change refers to changes in the overall climate, while global warming refers specifically to rising temperatures.</p>

<p>A <a href="https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315687391">historical review</a> found that, in the past, people were less likely to associate the term climate change with the idea that humans are actively warming the planet than they were with the term global warming. Perhaps this is why <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s10584-011-0070-4">Democrats used to like the term global warming,</a> while the popularization of the term climate change has been <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2003/03/02/us/a-call-for-softer-greener-language.html">credited to Frank Luntz</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315687391">an adviser to the George W. Bush</a> administration.</p>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s10584-010-9882-x">Past surveys</a> also found that Democrats used to think of global warming as being more serious than climate change, while Republicans thought of climate change as more serious than global warming. But <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jenvp.2020.101414">according to a recent review</a>, these partisan differences have now faded.</p>

<p><iframe id="IaVVC" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/IaVVC/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0"></iframe></p>

<p>Alternative terms such as climate crisis, climate emergency and climate justice have been used to emphasize other aspects of climate change and to try to raise concern. In 2019, the British newspaper <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2019/may/17/why-the-guardian-is-changing-the-language-it-uses-about-the-environment">The Guardian</a> switched to using climate crisis and climate emergency because it wanted to convey urgency.</p>

<p>Activists use the term climate justice to draw attention to climate change as a human rights challenge: Low-income people around the world <a href="https://theconversation.com/heat-waves-hit-the-poor-hardest-calculating-the-rising-impact-on-those-least-able-to-adapt-to-the-warming-climate-175224">suffer the most</a> from the effects of climate change, despite being the least responsible for causing it.</p>

<h2>The takeaway: Avoid overheated language</h2>

<p>Right now, the terms climate crisis, climate emergency or climate justice are less familiar and elicit less concern than climate change or global warming.</p>

<p>Even if these terms become more commonplace, there is no guarantee that they will heighten concern or inspire action. In fact, studies have suggested that phrases like climate crisis <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/1533015X.2013.795836">could backfire</a> if they don’t resonate with people.</p>

<p>Our advice: Don’t make the mistake of using overheated language. Just stick with familiar terms that people understand – use global warming when referring to rising temperatures and climate change for overall changes in the climate.</p>

<p><em>This updates an article originally published <a href="https://theconversation.com/if-you-want-americans-to-pay-attention-to-climate-change-just-call-it-climate-change-235002">Aug. 12, 2024</a>, with a new study and discussions at the 2026 U.N. climate conference, COP31.</em></p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/296481/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
