body: Escalating the language might work in a rally, but the general public isn't as swayed by it, studies show
Erik McGregor/LightRocket via Getty Images You may be hearing phrases like “climate crisis,” “climate emergency” and “climate justice” a lot as the 2026 United Nations climate summit is underway
Secretary-General António Guterres , are using them to try to get across the urgent risks and consequences of climate change

The danger is real , but is using this language actually persuasive? It turns out that Americans are more familiar with – and more concerned about – climate change and global warming than they are about climate crisis, climate emergency or climate justice, according to a survey we conducted with a nationally representative sample of 5,137 Americans
Moreover, we found no evidence that the alternative terms increased people’s sense of urgency, willingness to support climate-friendly policies or willingness to act

The familiar terms – climate change and global warming – did at least as well, and sometimes better, than climate crisis and climate emergency in eliciting concern, perceived urgency and willingness to act
The phrase climate justice consistently tended to do worse, likely in part because it was the least familiar
These response patterns were similar among Republicans, Democrats and independents
Just keep it simple In our work as research psychologists , we have explored how Americans respond to the ways climate change is communicated and have uncovered a need to use straightforward language

For example, people we interviewed for a study published in 2021 felt that climate experts were talking over their heads with terms like “adaptation,” “mitigation,” “sustainability” and “carbon-dioxide removal.” They wanted experts to use more familiar terms instead
This inspired us to write a quick guide to climate jargon , published in The Conversation
Using everyday language makes information easier to understand, and even highly educated people tend to prefer it
Jargon like “ biodiversity loss ” has similar problems
That refers to the shrinking variety of life on Earth, which is exacerbated by climate change

A survey of 7,338 U.S. adults led by one of us found people were much more familiar with and more concerned about “extinction of plants and animals” – or, if an explanation was provided, “nature loss”
Even with an explanation, “biodiversity loss” was the least familiar and of least concern for people among several terms
Most people didn’t find “biodiversity crisis” or “extinction crisis” familiar either
Yet, experts often use complex jargon because it is familiar to them, and they may not realize it is unfamiliar to others
How the terms evolved It has become common to talk about climate change and global warming as if they have the same meaning, but there are differences
Climate change refers to changes in the overall climate, while global warming refers specifically to rising temperatures

A historical review found that, in the past, people were less likely to associate the term climate change with the idea that humans are actively warming the planet than they were with the term global warming
Perhaps this is why Democrats used to like the term global warming, while the popularization of the term climate change has been credited to Frank Luntz , an adviser to the George W
Past surveys also found that Democrats used to think of global warming as being more serious than climate change, while Republicans thought of climate change as more serious than global warming
But according to a recent review , these partisan differences have now faded
Alternative terms such as climate crisis, climate emergency and climate justice have been used to emphasize other aspects of climate change and to try to raise concern
In 2019, the British newspaper The Guardian switched to using climate crisis and climate emergency because it wanted to convey urgency

Activists use the term climate justice to draw attention to climate change as a human rights challenge: Low-income people around the world suffer the most from the effects of climate change, despite being the least responsible for causing it
The takeaway: Avoid overheated language Right now, the terms climate crisis, climate emergency or climate justice are less familiar and elicit less concern than climate change or global warming
Even if these terms become more commonplace, there is no guarantee that they will heighten concern or inspire action
In fact, studies have suggested that phrases like climate crisis could backfire if they don’t resonate with people
Our advice: Don’t make the mistake of using overheated language
Just stick with familiar terms that people understand – use global warming when referring to rising temperatures and climate change for overall changes in the climate

<title>Debate in New York City over city-run groceries is not just about food, but something bigger</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771653/original/file-20261112-64-qfy0aq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C6602%2C4401&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Five city-run groceries in a city of 8 million won&#39;t substantially lower food prices, but the experiment might cause shoppers to think differently about the role of government.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/new-york-city-mayor-zohran-mamdani-holds-up-bananas-as-he-news-photo/2287861148?phrase=Mamdani%20grocery&amp;adppopup=true">Spencer Platt/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>New York City is moving closer to launching its effort to counter food inflation by opening five city-run grocery stores. <a href="https://www.nyc.gov/mayors-office/news/2026/05/mayor-mamdani-announces-the-peninsula-in-the-bronx-as-the-second">Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced in May 2026</a> that the first store would open in the Hunts Point neighborhood of the South Bronx in 2027, with another in East Harlem to follow. </p>

<p>Five stores, one in each borough, are unlikely to substantially change grocery prices in a city with <a href="https://www.nyc.gov/assets/foodpolicy/downloads/pdf/NYC-Food-by-the-Numbers-2025.pdf">nearly 1,000 supermarkets</a> and more than <a href="https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/newyorkcitynewyork">8 million inhabitants</a>. But each could make a meaningful difference to the grocery bills of local shoppers by selling essentials at below-market prices.</p>

<p>Even with just five planned stores set to open in lower-income neighborhoods, the initiative has ignited fierce opposition from <a href="https://www.courthousenews.com/nyc-grocers-sue-city-over-subsidized-municipal-grocery-stores-plan/">independent grocers</a>, <a href="https://www.grocerydive.com/news/new-york-city-municipal-grocery-stores-lawsuit-multicultural-business-coalition/828660/">supermarket trade associations</a> and a <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/newyork/news/nyc-city-run-grocery-store-lawsuit/">coalition representing immigrant-owned food businesses</a>. </p>

<p>What explains this pushback?</p>

<p>As a <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=VBgW-tsAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">food policy scholar</a>, I believe this opposition is about more than the immediate economic impact of five stores. It is about the precedent they could establish. Mamdani’s initiative challenges an entrenched expectation that the government should leave the provision of consumer goods to private enterprise even as it encourages businesses to invest in certain locations, regulates their activities and helps low-income shoppers through various food assistance programs. </p>

<p>The reality is more complicated. For at least a century, New York’s food economy has <a href="https://www.vitalcitynyc.org/government-is-already-in-the-grocery-business/">not operated independently of government</a>. In fact, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-publhealth-052220-021059">public policies and investments</a> have long shaped where supermarkets open, which businesses can operate with a profit, and how residents obtain food. </p>

<p>It’s just that they have done so in ways consumers often don’t see.</p>

<p>That is why the five grocery stores carry a broader significance, in my view. They offer a different model of public investment that makes the government much more visible in providing an essential service – and more accountable for its results. New Yorkers will get an opportunity to judge that contribution directly. </p>

<p>If the stores succeed, they may change not just what people expect to pay for groceries, but what they expect their city government to provide.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A man wearing in a turban and pushing a dolly walks by a grocery store in the Queens neighborhood of Jackson Heights, which has a large South Asian community." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771743/original/file-20261112-64-ecse3m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771743/original/file-20261112-64-ecse3m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=405&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771743/original/file-20261112-64-ecse3m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=405&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771743/original/file-20261112-64-ecse3m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=405&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771743/original/file-20261112-64-ecse3m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=509&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771743/original/file-20261112-64-ecse3m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=509&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771743/original/file-20261112-64-ecse3m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=509&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Some immigrant owners of New York grocery stores have warned that city-run alternatives will undercut them.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/general-views-of-the-indian-community-of-the-jackson-news-photo/53089295?phrase=indian%20grocery%20store%20new%20york&amp;adppopup=true">Scott Gries/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>How the plan will work</h2>

<p>New York City has <a href="https://edc.nyc/program/nyc-groceries">committed US$70 million</a> to develop these stores, which will be open to all.</p>

<p>While they will be managed by private operators, the city will provide rent-free space, prioritize publicly owned sites and ensure that essential foods are priced <a href="https://www.nyc.gov/mayors-office/news/2026/07/transcript-_mayor-mamdani-unveils-30--discount---including-all-p">30% below</a> typical retail prices. </p>

<p>In this respect, the stores offer a “<a href="https://democracyjournal.org/magazine/56/reviving-public-action/">public option</a>” – a <a href="https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/politics-policy-and-public-options/78B6D051FD7EEF9990D289CCE61EEE2F">government-provided good or service that exists alongside private alternatives</a>, like public schools and city hospitals. </p>

<p>Municipal grocery stores would offer New Yorkers a similar choice alongside private retailers. But as a public option, they would create a visible alternative against which shoppers can judge privately owned stores, setting a benchmark for food prices and service quality. They would also demonstrate how public investment can be used to make an essential good more affordable.</p>

<p>At his <a href="https://www.nyc.gov/mayors-office/news/2026/05/transcript--mayor-mamdani-announces-the-peninsula-in-the-bronx-a">May announcement</a>, Mamdani described the proposed Bronx store and its surrounding development as “physical proof of our conviction that government can be a force for good.” </p>

<h2>A fresh form of intervention</h2>

<p>Government-supported food retailing has a long history in New York City despite opposition by existing businesses. </p>

<p>In 1934, Mayor Fiorello La Guardia’s administration began <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1934/06/15/archives/19946-quarts-sold-of-city-milk-in-day-11151-families-get-supply-at.html">selling discounted milk</a> to low-income families, but the initiative drew complaints from grocers about unfair competition. Independent merchants similarly protested the city’s efforts to subsidize a new <a href="https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/1995/05/29/the-political-supermarket">Pathmark supermarket in East Harlem</a> in the 1990s, warning that it would put local grocers out of business. </p>

<p>A more recent example is the city’s <a href="https://edc.nyc/program/food-retail-expansion-support-health-fresh">Food Retail Expansion to Support Health program</a>, known as FRESH. Since 2009, it has offered supermarket developers and operators long-term tax breaks and <a href="https://www.jstor.org/content/oa_chapter_edited/j.ctv513dv1.23?seq=1">zoning incentives</a> to build or expand dozens of stores in underserved neighborhoods. </p>

<p>These incentives have helped increase grocery retail space, but shoppers don’t see the public support behind them. </p>

<p>FRESH is just one example of an approach toward <a href="https://ir.lawnet.fordham.edu/ulj/vol45/iss4/5/">supermarket financing</a> that gained momentum in the 1990s, when governments sought to address social problems by encouraging private investment. Food insecurity was <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/1468-2427.12515">blamed on a scarcity of</a> neighborhood supermarkets, not on prices being beyond reach for local shoppers. </p>

<p>Subsidizing new stores promised better nutrition and economic development without confronting poverty or inequality, and FRESH reflects that approach. Participating supermarkets must devote space to perishable foods, but they’re not required to offer affordable prices. That may be one reason why <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/s1368980017000933">researchers have found</a> that adding supermarkets to low-income neighborhoods, by itself, doesn’t substantially improve residents’ diets.</p>

<p>This hidden government role is hardly confined to grocery stores. Much of what government does for Americans is delivered indirectly, through tax credits, subsidies and private institutions. Because the public contribution is obscured, people often give credit to private markets for the benefits provided by public policy, from student loans to healthcare. </p>

<p>This invisibility is a consequence of policy design and influences how citizens understand government, a phenomenon that political scientist Suzanne Mettler described as “<a href="https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/S/bo12244559.html">the submerged state</a>.” </p>

<h2>Bringing the state into the open</h2>

<p>Municipal grocery stores depart from the traditional model in two important ways. </p>

<p>First, they make affordability an explicit condition of public investment rather than the outcome of increased retail competition. Second, they make government’s contribution visible. For example, the stores will share <a href="https://edc.nyc/press-release/nycedc-selects-branding-design-team-develop-visual-identity-nyc-groceries">distinct branding</a> so shoppers know who’s responsible for the affordable food. </p>

<p>If the stores deliver reliable savings, shoppers may begin to see affordable food as something government can help provide, not an outcome determined entirely by private markets. When public benefits are obscured, people are more likely to underestimate government’s contribution to their lives. Visible programs, like a physical store in the neighborhood, make that contribution easier to notice and evaluate.</p>

<p>Visibility also creates accountability. A customer at a private supermarket that received a tax break to expand isn’t likely to tie the store’s prices or food quality to government policy. At a municipal grocery store, with clear branding, the connection is unmistakable. </p>

<p>To be sure, critics’ concerns deserve serious attention. Many independent grocery stores are owned by immigrant entrepreneurs operating on thin margins. Groups representing bodegas and independent supermarkets warn that a publicly subsidized competitor could draw away their customers. Some may lose business. </p>

<p>Yet East Harlem’s Pathmark demonstrates that new supermarkets and smaller retailers can coexist. Between 2000 and 2015, the number of small grocery stores and bodegas in the neighborhood <a href="https://cunyurbanfoodpolicy.org/resources/report/eating-in-east-harlem/">increased from 100 to 126</a>, while supermarkets rose from 10 to 18. That said, those figures don’t establish Pathmark’s effects on individual businesses. </p>

<p>The municipal stores’ impact on nearby retailers remains an open question. But the task for New York City is to ensure that private operators deliver excellent service and real savings, and that their commercial interests don’t undermine the public mission. It will also need to provide good working conditions and track effects on nearby businesses.</p>

<p>Ultimately, public ownership doesn’t guarantee success. But it makes government’s responsibility for the outcome impossible to miss.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291749/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: Do the Dems need new leadership?
excerpt: Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) speaks during a news conference on Capitol Hill in June 2026. | Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images This story appeared in  Tod
body: Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) speaks during a news conference on Capitol Hill in June 2026. | Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images This story appeared in  Today, Explained,  a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here

Hi readers, happy Friday! Today, we’re saying farewell — for now — to “Democrats in array.” Not quite two weeks after winning the 2026 midterms by a historic margin , the party has a leadership fight on its hands.  On Thursday evening, Sen

Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, made it official: He’s challenging current Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer for the title of majority leader next year, promising a bolder and more aggressive agenda for the party.  “It is about answering the call of the American people,” Van Hollen told MS NOW host Jen Psaki when he announced his candidacy on her show. “The call was really to reject the status quo and to reject business as usual

And to do that, I think we need new leadership.” Newly elected Democrats Abdul El-Sayed (D-MI) and Peggy Flanagan (D-MN), each of whom defeated more leadership-aligned Democrats in their Senate primaries, are backing his bid
But Van Hollen will have an uphill climb to win the job, which is set to be decided in a closed-door vote early next month
Schumer, 75, has led Senate Democrats for nearly a decade, starting in 2017, and says he’s confident he will have the votes to be reelected in December
Searching for “fighters” The Senate is the only chamber currently dealing with an active leadership fight, but it’s not the only one with some leadership angst
In the House, current Democratic minority leader Hakeem Jeffries is the overwhelming favorite to become the new speaker in January (he currently lacks any Democratic challengers)

But not everyone is happy about it, as my colleague Astead Herndon reported on Thursday .  The divide, he argues — both in the Schumer-Van Hollen showdown and frustrations with Jeffries — is not really about progressive versus moderate

Instead, he says, it’s about an energized, angry Democratic base looking for fighters to lead the party into what’s almost certain to be a combative final two years of the Trump administration, and a sense that neither Schumer nor Jeffries are ready to meet the moment.  It’s not just a problem for this cycle, either: Democrats won so widely last week that they’re very likely to hang onto their majorities at least through the 2028 election,  Eric Levitz points out .  There’s nothing to say that Democrats will have the same leaders in two years (particularly Schumer, who’s up for reelection in 2028 but may either retire or face a serious primary challenge).  But the intra-party debate that we’re watching play out right now is effectively a preview of the higher-stakes fight to come in 2028, when Democrats could also have control of the presidency — and their freest legislative hand since the 2008 election.  As Eric writes , that will come with some real challenges, not least that Democrats currently appear to be facing an impossible trio of economic promises, one of which they’ll likely need to break
But it will also be a moment of opportunity — if the party’s leaders are ready for it

title: Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility
excerpt: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for i
body: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.” Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China

It is one of three chip-security bills under consideration for inclusion in the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, each of which is drawing renewed attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy
When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed

In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.” But privately, Nvidia representatives working with Foster told the lawmaker that the company could implement them. “They never put anything in writing,” Foster says, but during technical discussions on the possibility of such safeguards, their reaction was “yeah, of course we can do this.” This private acknowledgment to Foster goes further than anything Nvidia has previously made public
Other technology Nvidia has built for its customers suggests that the company can indeed offer accurate tracking of its chips’ locations
In December 2025, for example, it announced a new tool called Fleet Intelligence that would allow customers to monitor how its advanced chips were performing across different data center locations
In doing so, the tool could indicate which country chips were in, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters, but the company would not elaborate on whether this technology could be used to prevent smuggling
Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment or confirmation of Foster’s characterization

In early October, when lawmakers were reportedly increasingly concerned about Nvidia’s role in smuggling, MIT Technology Review asked the company if Fleet Intelligence could be used to prevent the practice

It declined to answer directly, instead sending a statement: “Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has.” The recent fallout at Nvidia involves a number of people and companies alleged to be involved in chip smuggling
Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair, runs Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm now under investigation for smuggling advanced GPUs to China
A US Commerce Department inquiry into the company was reportedly halted after invention by Nvidia

Megaspeed reportedly bought chips from Supermicro, a company that packages Nvidia’s chips onto servers.  The Chip Security Act as drafted would require a mechanism to track the locations of chips, either by inspections of facilities, attestations by companies, or ping-based location mechanisms
The ping-based technique, the hardest option to circumvent, would require the GPU to send a signal of its location when it comes online
In September, the Center for Security and Emerging Technology found it would be the most cost-effective option
Foster said he did not ask Nvidia’s representatives why they weren’t voluntarily adopting such chip-tracking tools if they could technically do so

But if the requirements of the bill pass as part of the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, the new tracking mechanisms would only tell investigators where the chips are, not offer a way to disconnect them if it’s revealed they have been smuggled
Foster told MIT Technology Review he intends to introduce new, stricter legislation in the new year that would offer a workaround

The new rule would require licenses to operate advanced GPUs, and before a GPU could connect, its valid license would need to be verified.   In the meantime, the controversy at Nvidia, Foster says, has fueled support among his colleagues for the rules in the bill: “There will be a lot of political pressure, in the wake of everything that’s happened, on the companies to actually do a very good job of the geographic validation of where the chip actually is.”

title: What to know about this year’s UN climate talks
excerpt: A charged atmosphere in Antalya: COP31 is unfolding against a backdrop of war, spiking energy prices, and a world already blowing past the 1.5 °C warming thresh
body: A charged atmosphere in Antalya: COP31 is unfolding against a backdrop of war, spiking energy prices, and a world already blowing past the 1.5 °C warming threshold the Paris Agreement was designed to prevent
The money problem: Rich nations promised $300 billion a year by 2035 for climate action, but delivered less than half that in 2024

Fossil fuels back in the spotlight: After last year's final agreement didn't mention "fossil fuels" once, expect a fight over language—especially with cohosts Australia and Turkey both deeply tied to coal and gas. " data-chronoton-post-id="1148308" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> It’s that time of year again: Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists are gathered for the annual UN climate talks, taking place this time in Antalya, Turkey
COP31 officially kicked off on November 8, marking the beginning of negotiations on one of the biggest stages of the climate world
Turkey and Australia are cohosting this year’s talks, which are scheduled to wrap up on November 20
This annual gathering can often serve as an indicator of where the world stands on addressing and adapting to the climate crisis
And this year’s talks are sure to be a doozy—expect a lot of back and forth on fossil fuels and climate finance in particular

Here’s what you should know about COP31.   In recent years, the tension always feels high when COP rolls around. (COP stands for “Conference of the Parties.”) But this year feels especially charged: The world is still grappling with the ongoing war in Iran, which has disrupted the Middle East and sent economic shock waves around the world as energy prices have spiked
This year’s COP will be the second without a formal delegation from the US
President Trump formally withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement earlier this year and is in the process of withdrawing from the UN Framework Committee on Climate Change

That’s the treaty that allows formal participation in negotiations.  Meanwhile, things aren’t looking good for the Paris Agreement, which was established at UN climate talks 11 years ago, setting a goal of limiting warming to 1.5 °C over preindustrial levels

In a report published in September, the UN Environment Program acknowledged that global warming is set to exceed that 1.5 °C goal, “likely within the next few years.” So as climate talks kick off, there’s an obvious, urgent question looming about how to quickly cut emissions to limit warming

There’s also the major issue of how to pay for efforts to address emissions and to help a warming world endure the inevitable damage.  Two years ago, talks ended in a goal of mobilizing $300 billion per year by 2035 to help pay to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. (Rich nations provided $136.7 billion in 2024, according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. ) And last year, the COP30 agreement included a goal of tripling the money for adaptation over that period. (Such funding has been quite flat over the past few years.) The world got a tragic reminder of just how high the stakes are earlier this year, when a glacier collapse caused devastating flooding in the Himalayas
The flood killed approximately 1,500 people, left over 5,000 missing, and caused nearly $5 billion in damage
The UN loss and damages fund committed $20 million to helping Nepal recover (less than 1% of the total estimated cost to the country)
Another key trend to watch is how the formal negotiations engage with the topic of fossil fuels
Three years ago, the final agreement text explicitly called for a transition away from them
But it felt as if things took a step back last year, when the final agreement didn’t even mention the phrase “fossil fuels” once

This will be an interesting conversation, especially because cohosts Turkey and Australia have both faced criticism over their relationships with these fuels—Australia is a major exporter of coal and natural gas, and Turkey’s grid relies heavily on fossil fuels, including coal
Outside the formal negotiations, COP31 president Murat Kurum, Turkey’s environment minister, is spearheading a side agenda, including two informal initiatives that will be worth watching

These wouldn’t be part of the official agreement text, but countries could sign on to signal support.   One is a pledge to make AI more sustainable; this is almost comically squishy, even as voluntary COP pledges go
The text includes explicit wording that it creates no new obligations for countries, so don’t expect anything resembling enforcement there
The COP leadership is also pushing to make electricity a larger part of member countries’ energy use
Today, only about 23% of global energy is used in the form of electricity
Fossil fuels, like gasoline in vehicles or natural gas for heating, make up the bulk of the rest
Shifting to more electricity use, and relying on cleaner sources for that electricity, could help drive down emissions

The new pledge’s target is for electricity to make up 35% of total energy consumption by 2035.  With leadership billing this as an “implementation COP,” it would be great to see some real, tangible progress on the global challenge of addressing climate change
I’m not expecting anything groundbreaking, but we’ll be tuned in to see what the final agreement shapes up to be.  This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter
